The marks on his shoe and the smell of medicine told Holmes everything.
Holmes said Watson only saw the stairs, and then showed him a note.
The paper came from Bohemia, and soon horses stopped outside the door.
A very tall man in rich furs and a black mask came in.
Holmes named the visitor as the King, and the man pulled off his mask.
Years ago the King knew a singer named Irene Adler.
The King had tried to get the photograph back, but he had failed.
Holmes agreed to help, and the King put money on the table.
Holmes dressed as a groom and learned that a lawyer visited Irene.
The lady went after him, and Holmes followed them both.
Holmes was pulled to the altar and signed as a witness.
Holmes asked Watson to help him with a plan.
Holmes, dressed as a priest, fell down outside the house.
Watson threw in a smoke rocket and shouted that there was a fire.
Holmes knew where the photograph was, and the two men walked home.
The next morning, Irene was gone from the house.
Holmes opened the hiding place and found only a letter and a picture.
Irene wrote that she had seen through Holmes's trick.
Holmes asked for Irene's picture, and he never forgot her.
One day Watson found Holmes with a fat visitor with red hair.
Holmes showed how a pin and a worn sleeve told so much.
Wilson kept a small shop, and his helper loved taking photographs.
Spaulding showed the notice and said Wilson should apply.
A crowd of red-haired men filled the street, and Spaulding led the way.
A small red-haired man pulled Wilson's hair to see whether it was real.
Wilson had to copy a book from ten until two each day.
For eight weeks he went each morning and was paid every Saturday.
One day the door was shut, and a card said the League was gone.
Holmes asked about the helper, and then he began to think.
Holmes tapped the street with his stick and then knocked at the door.
Holmes asked the way to the Strand and looked at the man's knees.
Holmes said the men were digging a tunnel to the bank.
That night Holmes, Watson and two other men rode to the bank.
Under the bank there was a cellar full of boxes of gold.
After a long wait in the dark, a light shone through the floor.
Holmes struck the thief's wrist, and the thief dropped his gun.
Jones named the thief as John Clay and led him away.
At home Holmes explained how he had understood the whole plan.
Holmes said that cases like this made life worth living.
A woman stood in the street, then she crossed to the door.
The woman came in and said that her fiancé was missing.
Mary lived with her mother and a stepfather who was young.
At a ball Mary met Hosmer Angel, a shy man in glasses.
Hosmer walked with Mary and wrote her letters on a typewriter.
At the church the cab was empty, and Hosmer was gone.
Holmes read the letters and told Mary to forget him.
Holmes wrote a short note and asked Windibank to call.
Holmes locked the door and told Windibank what he had done.
Windibank ran away, and Holmes did not tell Mary the truth.
A telegram came from Lestrade, and Watson's wife said he should go.
The train carried them west, and Lestrade met them at Ross.
Lestrade told them about two men who once lived in Australia.
A girl in the wood saw the father and the son argue.
James said his father spoke two strange words before he died.
Alice Turner said that James could not have done it.
Holmes thought about the cry and the two last words.
Holmes studied the ground by the pool very closely.
Holmes found a cigar end and a stone with a mark.
Lestrade laughed at Holmes, but Holmes was sure he was right.
Holmes went to see Turner, who was old and ill.
Holmes told Turner that he knew who had killed McCarthy.
Turner said that long ago he was a thief in Australia.
McCarthy held Turner's secret and made him give him a house.
Turner met McCarthy at the pool and they had a bitter quarrel.
Turner went back to take his cloak before the police came.
Holmes said he would only use the paper if James was found guilty.
At the trial, James was found not guilty, and he was free.
Turner died in peace, and the young couple were happy.
On the train home, Holmes thought of Turner and felt sad.
In a storm, a wet young man came to see Holmes.
Openshaw's uncle came home from America and kept a room locked.
A letter came from India with five orange seeds inside.
The old man burned his papers, and soon he was found dead.
The father got the same letter, and he was found dead.
Now John had the same letter, and he was afraid.
Holmes read a burned page and understood what the letters meant.
Holmes told Openshaw what to do, and he went home.
In the morning, Openshaw was dead, and Holmes was angry.
The ship was wrecked in a storm before Holmes could stop it.
A frightened woman came to Watson's door late at night.
Watson went in a cab to a dark, dirty street in the East End.
Watson found Whitney in a bunk and sent him home.
An old man pulled his sleeve and spoke to him quietly.
The old man was really Holmes, and he smiled at Watson.
Holmes drove to a big house, and a woman met them.
Mrs St Clair said that her husband had left for London.
She saw her husband at a window, and then he was gone.
She ran up the stairs, but two men stopped her.
The police found a poor man with a twisted lip in the room.
The police found blood by the window and a coat in the river.
Mrs St Clair showed Holmes a note from her husband.
Holmes sat up all night and woke Watson at dawn.
They drove to the police station and met Inspector Bradstreet.
Holmes asked for water and a sponge to wash the sleeper's face.
The man's face came clean, and it was Neville St Clair.
St Clair was ashamed and asked to keep the secret.
St Clair said begging paid him more than writing for a newspaper.
St Clair went on begging, and he kept it secret from his wife.
He saw his wife, threw his coat in the river, and hid.
Watson found Holmes on a sofa, looking at an old hat.
A man dropped his goose and his hat and ran away.
A card on the goose gave a name, but a common one.
Holmes read the hat and told Watson about its owner.
Then Peterson ran in and showed a blue stone.
Holmes said it was a famous stone with a big reward.
A plumber was arrested for stealing the jewel from a hotel.
Holmes locked up the stone and said that the goose held the secret.
Holmes wrote a notice in the paper for Henry Baker.
Baker took his hat, and he told Holmes where the goose came from.
Holmes and Watson went out into the cold night.
At the Alpha Inn, the landlord told Holmes where the geese came from.
At the market, Holmes found a man at a stall.
Holmes made a bet, and the man showed his book.
A small man asked about the geese, and Holmes spoke to him.
Holmes took Ryder to Baker Street and showed him the stone.
Ryder cried, and he said that he was sorry.
Ryder told how he put the stone into a goose.
Holmes let Ryder go, and the little man ran off.
Holmes said that Christmas was a time for forgiving.
A frightened lady came to see Holmes very early.
Helen lived at Stoke Moran with her stepfather in a grey, old house.
Roylott went to India, and he came home an angry man.
The mother died, and the girls lived in the old house.
Julia was going to be married, but she heard a whistle at night.
Julia screamed about a speckled band and she died.
Now Helen was going to marry, and she heard the same whistle.
Holmes saw marks on Helen's wrist and said that he would come.
After Helen left, a huge man came into the room.
Roylott bent the poker, and Holmes bent it straight.
In the house, Holmes found a strange rope above a bed.
In Roylott's room, Holmes saw a safe and a dish of milk.
Holmes and Watson waited at an inn near the house.
They climbed in and waited in the dark room.
A light came through the vent, and Holmes struck the rope.
A terrible cry came, and they ran to Roylott's room.
Roylott sat dead in his chair with a yellow band on him.
Holmes caught the snake and locked it in the iron safe.
Holmes told Watson how he had guessed the whole plot.
Helen was safe, and Holmes said Roylott had caused his own death.
A pale young man with a hurt hand came to Watson.
Hatherley was a poor young engineer with few clients.
The stranger offered a great deal of money for one night's work.
At the little station, a carriage was waiting for him.
At the house, a woman told him to run away.
Stark showed him a big iron machine and asked about a leak.
Hatherley saw that the machine pressed metal, not earth.
Stark locked Hatherley in, and the roof of the press began to come down.
A woman opened a hidden panel, and he got out.
Hatherley hung from a window and lost his thumb.
Hatherley woke in the garden at dawn with a very sore hand.
He walked slowly down the lane to find the railway station.
At the station he took the first train to London.
At Baker Street, Holmes listened and then read a notice about a missing engineer.
Holmes looked at a map and said the house must be near Eyford.
They took a train with a police inspector and another man.
At Eyford they saw black smoke rising over the trees.
Hatherley cried, “That is the house,” and they all ran up the hill.
Holmes found the marks of a man and a woman leading away.
Hatherley said he had lost his thumb and his money.
Holmes read a letter from a lord who wanted his help.
Lord St Simon came and told of the wedding at the church.
A stranger gave back the bride's flowers when she dropped them.
The bride went upstairs, put on a coat, and left the house.
Holmes asked about the bride, and the lord answered proudly.
Lestrade brought a wet bundle from the water in the park.
Lestrade thought a woman had pushed the bride into the water.
Holmes ordered a cold supper and said the answer was simple.
Hatty and her first husband came in and told the story.
The lord left in anger, and the lovers had a good supper.
A rich banker ran into Baker Street, pale and very afraid.
A famous lord left a gold crown with the banker.
Holder's son Arthur spent too much, and his friend was a bad one.
In the night, Holder heard a noise and went downstairs.
Arthur would not say a word, so Holder called the police.
Holmes and Holder went to Streatham to look at the house.
Holmes studied the marks in the snow outside the house.
Mary asked Holmes to save her cousin Arthur from prison.
Holmes went out in rough old clothes and came back late.
Mary had helped Burnwell, and Arthur had kept it secret.
Miss Violet Hunter came to Holmes with a strange job offer.
A cheerful, fat man offered her a great deal of money.
Rucastle said she must cut her hair and wear his dress.
Violet went to Copper Beeches and had her hair cut short.
Rucastle told funny stories while Violet sat by the window.
The family was strange, and a huge dog roamed the grounds.
Violet saw a man in the road by using a mirror.
In a drawer she found hair just like her own.
Part of the house was empty, and one door was locked.
Violet wanted the truth, and she sent a telegram to Holmes.
Holmes heard her tale and guessed that she was a stand-in.
Toller was asleep from drink, and Violet took his keys.
The locked room was empty, and a ladder stood below the roof window.
Mr Rucastle came home early and found them in the house.
Rucastle shouted for the dog, and the hungry beast jumped at him.
Toller shot the dog, and Rucastle lay hurt on the floor.
Toller told them that Alice was Rucastle's daughter.
Alice married Mr Fowler, and they sailed to an island far away.
Holmes watched the fields from the train and spoke quietly.
Watson looked at his notes and thought of his friend.
B1B2: Watson, now married, saw Holmes's shadow pacing behind a lit blind in Baker Street and climbed the stairs. After one glance, Holmes told him that he had gained seven and a half pounds and gone back to his work.

Holmes explained that the deep cuts on Watson's shoe had been made by a careless servant scraping off wet mud. The smell of medicine, and a bulge in the top hat where a stethoscope was hidden, had told him the rest.

Holmes pointed out that Watson had climbed the stairs hundreds of times without counting them, although there were seventeen steps. Then he handed him an unsigned note, which promised a visitor at a quarter to eight who would wear a mask.

Holmes held the paper to the lamp and showed that it had been made in Bohemia and written by a German. Just then horses' hoofs sounded in the street below, and Holmes whistled and said that there was money in the case.
A huge man came in, dressed in rich furs and heavy boots, with a black mask covering the top of his face. He said that Holmes might call him Count Von Kramm, a nobleman of Bohemia.

The visitor asked for two years of silence, and both men promised. Then Holmes calmly named him as Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, King of Bohemia, and the huge man tore the mask from his face.

Five years earlier, the King had known a famous singer called Irene Adler, and she now held a photograph of the two of them together. He was about to marry a princess from a strict family, and Irene had threatened to send it to them.

Holmes looked her up in his index and learned that she was an American opera singer, now living quietly in London. The King admitted that he had tried to steal the photograph back, but her house and luggage had been searched in vain.

Holmes agreed to take the case, and the grateful King placed three hundred pounds in gold and seven hundred in notes on the table. Holmes wrote the address of Briony Lodge on his shirt cuff and asked Watson to call at three the next day.

Next day Holmes, dressed as a rough groom, chatted with the grooms in the stable lane behind Briony Lodge. He learned that Irene Adler had only one regular visitor, a handsome young lawyer named Godfrey Norton.

Within minutes Irene Adler came out of the house, got into her own carriage and followed the lawyer at great speed. Holmes jumped into a cab and trailed them both to the Church of St Monica in the Edgware Road.

Godfrey Norton and Irene Adler were being married, and, since they needed a witness, Holmes was dragged to the altar and signed his name. Afterwards the bride gave him a golden sovereign, which he now wore on his watch chain.

Holmes said that he needed help, and Watson, who was never afraid of breaking the law in a good cause, agreed at once. The plan was simple: when the lady was carried into her sitting room, Holmes would raise his hand and Watson would act.

Holmes, in a broad black hat and white tie, was knocked down in a fight among street loafers outside Briony Lodge. His face was covered in red, and the lady's servants carried him into the sitting room.

Holmes raised his hand, and Watson threw the smoke rocket through the window and cried that the house was on fire. Smoke filled the room, and Irene ran to the bell pull where the photograph was hidden.

Holmes had learned what he wanted, and he slipped away while the servants searched for the fire. As they walked toward Baker Street, a slim young man in an overcoat passed them and said, good night, Mister Sherlock Holmes.

Next morning Holmes, Watson and the King went to Briony Lodge, where an old servant said that her mistress had left with her husband. They had gone to the Continent, and they were not coming back to England.

Holmes ran to the bell pull, tore back a small sliding panel and thrust in his hand. The photograph was gone, and there was only a picture of Irene Adler in evening dress and a letter addressed to himself.

Irene's letter said that Holmes had played the part very well, but she had been warned against him and knew his methods. She was a trained actress, she wrote, and she had put on a man's clothes and followed him home.

The King cried that Irene would have made a fine queen, and Holmes dryly replied that she was on a very different level. He refused a ring and asked for her photograph, and from then on he spoke of her as the woman.

Watson called on Holmes one autumn day and found him talking to a stout, red-faced old man with fiery hair. Holmes said that the stranger had done hard work with his hands, been to China and written a great deal lately.

Holmes explained that the right hand was larger than the left, so the man had worked with it. His shiny cuff showed writing, and a fish tattoo and a Chinese coin on his watch chain showed that he had been to China.

Wilson owned a small pawnbroker's shop in Saxe-Coburg Square, near the City, and he had only one helper. The man, Vincent Spaulding, worked for half wages and was fond of photography, which often took him down into the cellar.
One day Spaulding wished that he had red hair and showed Wilson a notice about the Red-Headed League. It offered four pounds a week to any red-haired man for work that was almost nothing.

Wilson had never expected to see so many red-haired men as he found in Fleet Street, in shades of orange, lemon, brick and flame. Spaulding pushed his master through the crowd and right up the stairs to the office.

In the office a little man with hair even redder than Wilson's introduced himself as Duncan Ross. He pulled Wilson's hair hard to make sure that it was not a wig, then cried that he was the man for the post.
His task was to copy out the Encyclopaedia Britannica in the office from ten until two every day. He could not leave the room during those hours, or he would lose the post for ever.

Every morning for eight weeks Wilson sat at the little table and copied, and every Saturday Ross paid him four golden sovereigns. He had written about Abbots, Archery, Armour, Architecture and Attica, and he hoped to reach the letter B before long.

Then one morning the office door was locked, with a small card that read, the Red-Headed League is dissolved. The landlord had never heard of the League, and Duncan Ross seemed to be a man who could not be found.
Holmes asked what Spaulding was like, and learned that he was small, quick and clean-shaven, with an acid scar on his forehead. Then Holmes lit his pipe and sat deep in thought for a long time.

After the concert Holmes and Watson walked to Saxe-Coburg Square, a poor little street of faded shops. Holmes struck the pavement hard with his stick, and then he knocked at the door of Wilson's shop.

Holmes asked the assistant the way to the Strand, and the young man answered at once and shut the door. Holmes remarked that he was the fourth smartest man in London, but he had only wished to look at his knees.

Holmes was now certain that the League was a trick to get Wilson out of his shop every morning. While the pawnbroker copied in Fleet Street, his assistant was digging a tunnel from the cellar to the vault of the bank.

That evening Holmes asked two men to join them: Peter Jones, a detective from Scotland Yard, and Mr Merryweather, a director of the bank. Merryweather was cross, because he was missing his weekly game of cards.
Merryweather led them down through iron gates into a great cellar filled with wooden cases. In them lay thirty thousand napoleons of French gold, which the bank had borrowed from the Bank of France.

They waited for what seemed hours in utter darkness, and Watson began to ache from sitting still. At last a spark of light appeared between two paving stones, and a white hand came up through the floor.
A man climbed out of the hole and helped a second man up after him. Holmes seized the first by the collar and, as he drew a pistol, struck his wrist with a hunting crop.

Jones knew the thief at once as John Clay, a murderer, thief and forger who had been to Eton and Oxford. His friend was caught at the shop end of the tunnel, and Clay calmly asked the police to say sir and please.

Back in Baker Street, Holmes told Watson that the strange advertisement could only have one purpose: to keep Wilson away. The assistant who took half wages, the cellar and the knees of his trousers had told him the rest.

Watson told him that he was a benefactor to the human race, and Holmes only shrugged. His life, he said, was one long effort to escape from the commonplaces of existence, and cases like these helped him do it.

Holmes and Watson sat by the window, and Holmes said that life is far stranger than anything people could invent. Just then a large woman in a feathered hat stopped in the street below and looked up at the house.

The visitor was Miss Mary Sutherland, and Holmes guessed at once that she earned her living by typing and that her eyes were weak. She admitted both, and then she said that her fiancé had vanished on his wedding morning.
Mary lived with her mother and her stepfather, Mr Windibank, who was only five years older than she was. He sold wine and often travelled to France, and he disliked her going out in the evening.
Mary went to a gasfitters' ball while her stepfather was in France, and there she met a quiet man named Hosmer Angel. He wore tinted glasses, spoke in a whisper and worked as a clerk in the City.

Hosmer called while Mr Windibank was away, walked with Mary in the evenings and wrote her typed letters, which he sent to the post office. He asked her to marry him quickly, before her stepfather came back from France.

On the wedding morning Mary and her mother drove to St Saviour's church in one cab, and Hosmer followed in another. When the second cab arrived at the church, the door was opened and the seat was empty.
Holmes looked at the letters, all typed, even the signature, and asked Mary for her stepfather's address. He told her to forget Hosmer Angel, but Mary replied that she would be true to him.
After Mary had gone, Holmes thought deeply and then wrote a polite note to Mr Windibank, asking him to call at Baker Street. He told Watson that the problem was easier than it looked.

Mr Windibank came, and Holmes compared the typing of his business letter with the letters from Hosmer Angel. He showed that the same machine had made the same small faults, locked the door and said that the stepfather had played the part himself.
Windibank said that Holmes could do nothing to him, for no law had been broken, and he ran down the stairs. Holmes did not tell Mary, because he knew that she would never believe him.

A telegram arrived from Inspector Lestrade, who asked Holmes to come to the west of England about a death at Boscombe Valley. He added that the air and the scenery were perfect, and Watson's wife told him to go.

Holmes read the newspapers all through the journey to Ross, in Herefordshire, and said little. Lestrade met them at the station and drove them to the inn, the Hereford Arms, where rooms were ready for them.

Lestrade explained that Charles McCarthy, the dead man, had rented a farm at Boscombe Valley from a rich landlord, John Turner. Both men had once lived in Australia, and they had been friends for a long time.

On the afternoon of the death, Charles McCarthy walked to Boscombe Pool, and soon afterwards his son followed him with a gun. A young girl who was picking flowers saw them quarrelling, and James seemed ready to strike his father.

James told the police that he had heard his father cry Cooee and had found him dying beside the pool. The dying man had said something about a rat, he added, and a grey cloak that he had seen on the ground was gone.
That evening Miss Alice Turner came to the inn and told Holmes that she had known James all her life. She was certain that he was innocent, and she begged them to find the truth.

At the inn, Holmes read the notes of the police and thought about the call of Cooee that the father had made. It was a call used in Australia, so the man he was expecting must have come from that country.
At the pool Holmes got down on the ground with a lens and studied every mark in the grass. He found the prints of the dead man, his son and a third man who had stood by a big stone.

Beside the stone he found the ash of a cigar and a mark on the stone where something heavy had been used. From the blow and the footprints, he said, the killer was tall, left-handed and lame in the right foot.

Holmes told Lestrade that the killer was a tall, limping man with a grey cloak, and that he would soon find him. Lestrade laughed, and said that he was a practical man and preferred a theory that fitted the boy.
The next day Holmes and Watson walked to John Turner's house, and Holmes asked to see him. The old landowner was tall and white-haired, with a limp and a grey cloak lying over the back of his chair.

Holmes told the old man quietly that he knew the whole story and wished to hear it from him. Turner covered his face with his hands, and then said that he was a dying man who had nothing left to hide.

Turner said that in his youth in Australia he had been the leader of a wild gang of robbers called Black Jack of Ballarat. They had attacked a wagon of gold, and a young driver named McCarthy had been among the men in the wagon.

McCarthy came to England and found Turner, and soon he held him in his power with the threat of telling everyone. He demanded a farm and an easy rent, and later he wanted Turner's daughter to marry his son.
Turner had agreed to meet McCarthy by the pool, hoping to beg him to stop. In a moment of rage he struck him a heavy blow and ran away into the trees.
James had arrived in time to hear his father's last words, and he had gone to fetch help. In that moment Turner returned, took up his cloak and went away into the wood.
Holmes said that he was not a policeman and would not betray a dying man, unless James was found guilty. Turner, whom the doctor had given only a few months, signed a written account of the crime.
At the trial the jury heard that there was little real evidence against James, and Holmes had shown where the police had gone wrong. James was found not guilty, and Alice cried for joy.
Turner lived for about seven months more and then died in his bed. James and Alice never learned of the dark cloud that hung over their fathers' past.

On the train home, Holmes thought sadly about Turner, who had made one terrible mistake in a hard life. Whenever he heard of such a case, he told Watson, he thought that there but for the grace of God goes Sherlock Holmes.

In September the winds howled round Baker Street, and Watson, whose wife was visiting her mother, was staying in his old rooms. Late in the evening a drenched young man named John Openshaw came in, begging for help.

Openshaw said that his uncle Elias had made a fortune as a planter in Florida and had then moved to a house near Horsham. He was a hard, silent man who kept the door of one attic room locked at all times.

In March 1883 a letter arrived for his uncle from Pondicherry in India, and inside it were five dried orange pips. When the old man saw the letters KKK on the paper, he turned deathly white and cried that his sins had caught him.
Elias burned the papers from a box in his attic, and then he made a will leaving the estate to Openshaw's father. Seven weeks later he was found dead in a shallow green pool in the garden.

In January 1885 Openshaw's father received an envelope with a Dundee postmark, five pips and an order to put the papers on the sundial. A few days later he was found dead at the foot of an old chalk pit, and the jury called it an accident.
John Openshaw inherited the farm, and for nearly three years nothing happened. Then, only the day before, a third envelope had come with five pips, and the police he had gone to had only laughed.

Openshaw had kept a scrap of paper from his uncle's fire, which spoke of pips that had been sent to three men. Holmes said that KKK stood for the Ku Klux Klan, a secret society of the American South, and that its members had come after Elias.
Holmes saw that the three letters came from three ports, and he told Openshaw to leave a note on the sundial. Openshaw thanked him, buttoned his coat and went out into the wild, wet night.

All night Holmes searched the shipping lists and found a ship that had been in all three ports, the Lone Star. In the morning the newspaper said that a young man named John Openshaw had been found drowned near Waterloo Bridge.

Holmes learned that the Lone Star had sailed from London that same day, and he sent a message to the harbour at Savannah. But the ship never arrived there, and some wreckage with the two letters L and S was found at sea.
One June night Watson's wife called him to the door, where an old friend, Kate Whitney, stood in tears. Her husband Isa had gone to an opium den in East London two days earlier and had not come home.

Watson drove to Upper Swandam Lane, a narrow, dirty alley near the river, and went down some steps into a smoky room. Men lay on bunks like sailors on a ship, staring or muttering, in the dim light of the lamp.
At last Watson found Isa Whitney, who was pale, thin and shaking, and he took him out into the fresh air. Watson put him in a cab, and then the old friend was driven home to his wife.

As Watson turned to leave, a hand pulled at his sleeve, and a low voice said that he should walk past and look back. It was an old, bent man in the corner who seemed to be half asleep, with a pipe in his hand.
The old man was Sherlock Holmes, who had been sitting in the den for days on a case. He had a trap waiting outside, and he asked Watson to drive with him to a house in Lee.
They drove out of London to The Cedars, a large villa standing in its own grounds at Lee. Mrs Neville St Clair received them in a light dress and begged them to find her husband.
Neville St Clair was a respectable man with a wife, two children and a good house, and he went to London every day. On Monday he told her he would buy a box of toy bricks for their small boy.
In Swandam Lane Mrs St Clair looked up and saw her husband at an upper window, waving his arms. His face was white, and then he was pulled back suddenly, as though by a hand from behind.
Mrs St Clair ran into the house, but a sailor from India and the owner pushed her out into the street. She ran to find help and met Inspector Bradstreet, who came with her.

In the room above the police found Hugh Boone, a well-known beggar of the City, with red hair and a scarred, twisted lip. Beside him lay the coat and clothes of Neville St Clair and the box of toy bricks.
There was blood on the window sill, and St Clair's coat lay in the river mud below, its pockets stuffed with coins. Without the weight of the coins, the tide would have carried it away.

Mrs St Clair showed Holmes a short note that she had received that morning in her husband's own writing. It told her not to be frightened, since all would come well, and asked her to wait in patience.
Holmes gathered all the cushions in the room and sat among them all night with his pipe, while Watson slept. At dawn he woke his friend, bright and laughing, and said that they must go at once.

In the cool of the morning Holmes drove them to Bow Street police station, where Inspector Bradstreet was already at work. Bradstreet, who knew and respected Holmes, agreed to let them see the prisoner in his cell.
Hugh Boone was lying asleep in the cell, a dirty, ugly man with red hair and a scarred, twisted lip. Holmes asked for a basin of water and a sponge, and Bradstreet gave them at once.
Holmes rubbed the beggar's face hard, and the scar came away, along with the whole wig of red hair. Underneath was a pale, sad, handsome face, and Bradstreet gasped that it was Neville St Clair.
The prisoner covered his face and agreed that he was Neville St Clair. He had done no harm to anyone, he said, and he begged them not to let his children learn that their father was a beggar.
St Clair told them that he had once been an actor and a newspaper reporter. For one article he dressed as a beggar and learned that he could earn more in a day than in a week at his desk.
Soon he found himself in debt, and begging seemed the only way to pay it off. He rented a room in Swandam Lane, where he could dress as Hugh Boone each day and change back each evening.
When St Clair saw his wife in the street, he hid and hurled his coat, heavy with coins, into the river. Bradstreet said that if Hugh Boone never appeared again, the police would let the matter rest.
Two days after Christmas, Watson called at Baker Street and found Holmes lying on the sofa in his purple dressing gown. Beside him, on a chair, lay a very old and battered felt hat.
The hat, said Holmes, had been brought to him by Peterson, a commissionaire. At four on Christmas morning Peterson had seen roughs attack a man with a goose, and the man ran away, leaving both.

A card was tied to the leg of the goose, reading For Mrs Henry Baker, and the letters H and B were inside the hat. There were hundreds of Bakers in London, so it was no easy matter to find the right one.

Holmes held the hat to the light and said that its owner was clever and had once been rich, but was poor now. He added that the man was middle-aged, with grey hair, and that there was no gas in his house.
Just then the door flew open, and Peterson dashed in, red in the face and gasping. He held out his hand, and in the palm lay a bright blue stone, which his wife had found in the goose.

Holmes took the stone between finger and thumb and said that it was the Blue Carbuncle, the most famous jewel in London. A reward of a thousand pounds had been offered for it, and he reached for the newspaper.

The stone had been stolen from the Countess's room at the Hotel Cosmopolitan on the twenty-second of December. A plumber named John Horner had been mending the grate there, and he had been arrested for the theft.
Holmes locked the stone in his strong box and said that the plumber might well be innocent. The goose had come from somewhere, he said, and the person who owned it might know how the stone got there.
Holmes wrote a short notice for the evening papers asking Mr Henry Baker to call at Baker Street at half past six for his hat. He sent Peterson to the newspapers, and then to buy a new goose.

At half past six Henry Baker arrived, a round-shouldered man with a large head and a pointed beard. Holmes gave him the hat and the new goose, and Baker said that the old one came from a goose club at the Alpha Inn.
When Baker had gone, Holmes said that the man knew nothing about the stone, and that they must trace the goose at once. He and Watson put on their coats and walked out into the frosty night.
At the Alpha Inn, Holmes ordered two glasses of beer and praised the landlord's geese. The landlord said that the geese came from a dealer in Covent Garden named Breckinridge.
Covent Garden market was nearly empty, and the stalls were being shut for the night. Holmes found Breckinridge, a sharp-faced man with sidewhiskers, closing the shutters of his stall.

Holmes offered to bet a sovereign that the bird was bred in the country, and Breckinridge, who knew better, brought out his book. It showed that the geese had come from a Mrs Oakshott of Brixton Road.

A small, ferret-faced man asked Breckinridge in a whining voice where a certain goose had gone, and the dealer lost his temper. Holmes followed the stranger into the street, and the man gave his name as James Ryder.
At Baker Street Holmes sat the little man by the fire and told him that the goose had been there. He took out the Blue Carbuncle, and Ryder stared at it like a man who sees a ghost.
Holmes told Ryder that he knew everything, from the maid's talk about the plumber to the empty jewel case. Ryder fell on his knees, begged for mercy and said that he had never been in trouble before.

Ryder said that after the theft he took the stone to his sister's house in Brixton, where she kept geese. He pushed it down the throat of a goose with a barred tail, but later he found that he had taken the wrong bird.
Holmes opened the door and told the pale man to leave at once. Ryder ran down the stairs and out into the street as fast as he could, and his feet were heard clattering along the pavement.
Holmes said that he was not paid to do the police's work, and that Christmas was a season for forgiveness. Horner would be free, and Ryder was too frightened ever to steal again.

Early one April morning Holmes woke Watson and said that a lady was waiting, so urgent that she had come before seven. She sat by the fire in a thick veil, and she said that it was fear that made her shiver.

Helen lived at Stoke Moran, in Surrey, with her stepfather, Dr Grimesby Roylott, the last of a once-rich family. The old house was falling to pieces, and the family's land had been sold, piece by piece.
Roylott had practised as a doctor in Calcutta, where he lost his temper and beat his servant to death. After a prison sentence he came back to England, and he was a hard and violent man.

Their mother died in a railway accident, and the money she left would go to Roylott as long as the girls lived with him. He shut himself in the house, quarrelled with every neighbour and kept a cheetah and a baboon in the grounds.
Two years earlier Julia, who was to be married soon, came to Helen's room at midnight and asked if she had heard a low whistle. Helen had not, and Julia went back, but she was very frightened.
That night Helen heard a scream and a clang of metal, and Julia staggered out of her room in terror. She cried out the words, the speckled band, and then she fell, and in a few minutes she was dead.

Now Helen herself was engaged to be married, and her stepfather had agreed. But workmen had begun repairs, and she had to sleep in Julia's old room, and the night before she had heard the same whistle.

Holmes noticed five small bruises on her white wrist and said that her stepfather had treated her cruelly. He promised that he and Watson would come to Stoke Moran that day, and she thanked him with tears in her eyes.
Soon after Helen left, the door was thrown open, and a huge man in a black coat and tall hat filled the doorway. It was Dr Roylott, who had followed her, and he glared at the two friends.
Roylott warned Holmes not to meddle, and to show his strength he seized the poker and bent it into a curve. Then he threw it into the grate and left, and Holmes smiled and bent it straight again.

At Stoke Moran, Holmes looked at the room where Helen slept and found a bell rope that was not joined to a bell. It hung beside a small vent that led to Roylott's room, and the bed was fixed to the floor.
In the doctor's bedroom, Holmes saw a small iron safe, a saucer of milk and a whip with a loop at the end. A wooden chair stood under the vent, and he looked at it thoughtfully.
Holmes told Helen to claim a headache, lock herself in her old room and light a lamp when Roylott went to bed. He and Watson took a room at the Crown Inn, which overlooked the house.
At eleven a bright lamp shone in the window, and the two men crossed the lawn and climbed into the dark room. They sat there with a cane and a pistol, and the village clock struck the quarter hours.

At about three in the morning, a glimmer of light shone through the vent, and a smell of burning oil filled the room. Then a gentle sound like steam from a kettle came, and Holmes sprang up and lashed at the rope with his cane.
A horrible cry came from the next room, the cry of pain, fear and anger all together. The two men ran into the passage and, after a moment, opened the door of Roylott's room.

Dr Roylott sat dead in his chair, his eyes fixed on the ceiling, and around his head was a strange yellow band with brown speckles. Holmes whispered that it was the speckled band, and the band began to move.
Holmes slipped the loop of the whip around the snake's neck and carried it at arm's length to the iron safe. He threw it in, shut the door, and said that the doctor had died within ten seconds.
Holmes explained that the bell rope, the vent and the saucer of milk had made him think of a snake. The doctor had trained the snake with milk and a whistle, and his own plan had killed him.

Helen went to stay with an aunt near Harrow, and Holmes said that he was indirectly responsible for the doctor's death. But he did not think it would weigh heavily on his conscience, for the doctor's own wicked plan had come back to destroy him.

Early one summer morning, a railway guard brought a pale young man to Watson's surgery in Paddington. The young man, Victor Hatherley, had a handkerchief wrapped round his hand, and he fainted soon after he sat down.
After Watson had bandaged the hand, Hatherley told his story. He had an office in Victoria Street but very little work, until a stranger called Colonel Lysander Stark came.

Colonel Stark offered fifty guineas for a single night's work, which was far more than the job was worth. He insisted on absolute secrecy and told Hatherley to take the last train to Eyford that very night.
At the small station of Eyford, Colonel Stark met him and led him to a closed carriage waiting in the dark. The windows were made of frosted glass, so that Hatherley could not see anything outside.
When the carriage stopped, Hatherley was led into a lonely house with a dark hall. A woman appeared with a lamp and whispered in broken English that he should go away at once.
Colonel Stark led him into a large room that held a huge hydraulic press, which he said was used to press fuller's earth into bricks. The machine was leaking, and he asked Hatherley to find out why.

While he mended the leak, Hatherley saw a shining crust of metal on the floor of the press. This told him that the machine was used to press metal, and a gang of coiners must be using it for false coins.
Stark pushed him into the little room, locked the door and started the machine. The heavy iron roof began to come down slowly toward Hatherley, and he knew that he would be crushed.
At the very last moment the woman from the hall slid back a small panel in the wall. Hatherley threw himself through it, and a moment later the roof came down with a crash behind him.
Hatherley climbed out of the window and hung from the sill by his fingers, but Stark ran up with a heavy cleaver. The blow cut off his thumb, and he dropped into the garden below and lost his senses.

When he woke, it was dawn, and he was lying in wet grass beneath a hedge with his hand bleeding badly. He bound his handkerchief tightly round the stump, but the pain was so sharp that he almost fainted again.
He climbed to his feet and staggered out of the garden into a quiet country lane. Following the road as well as his weak legs would let him, he made his way back toward the railway.
At Eyford station he caught the first train of the morning and changed at Reading. By the time he reached Paddington, he was so weak that a kind railway guard had to help him.
At Baker Street, Holmes sat among his heaps of newspapers and listened with great attention. Then he read out an old notice about a missing engineer called Hayling, who was never seen again.
Hatherley said that the horses had seemed to run for an hour, but Holmes was not so sure. He thought that the carriage had only gone round and round, so the house might lie close to the station.

Holmes sent a note to Inspector Bradstreet of Scotland Yard, who met them at Paddington with a plain-clothes man. The five of them took the next train for Eyford, and Holmes spread his map on his knees.
When they stepped down at Eyford, a great column of black smoke was rising behind the trees. A porter told them that a house on the hill was on fire, and Hatherley cried out in alarm.

The house stood at the top of a rise, and flames had already burst through the upper windows. Villagers were passing buckets of water from hand to hand, but it was plain that nothing could save the building.

Holmes learned from the villagers that the fire had begun in a downstairs room, probably when a lamp had been knocked over. In the soft earth of the garden, he found the prints of a heavy man and a small woman leaving together.

On the way home, Hatherley said sadly that he had lost his thumb and his fee, and had gained nothing. Holmes laughed and told him that he had gained a story, which would make him good company for life.
One wet afternoon, Holmes read a letter from Lord Robert St Simon, which bore a great coat of arms. It said that the lord would call at four o'clock about a wedding that had gone wrong.

Lord St Simon was a tall, proud man with a stern mouth and an old-fashioned way of speaking. He said that the wedding had been very quiet, with only a few guests, at St George's Church in Hanover Square.

As she left the church, the bride dropped her flowers, and a gentleman in the front pew handed them back. Later a dancer named Flora Millar, an old friend of the lord, forced her way in and made a scene.
While the guests were at breakfast, Hatty slipped upstairs and came down again in a long coat and a bonnet. A maid saw her walk out of the front door, and no one saw her come back.

Holmes asked about the lady's past, and the lord said that she had grown up in the wild mining camps of the West. He seemed hurt in his pride rather than in his heart, and he left as soon as Holmes had finished.
Soon afterward, Inspector Lestrade came in with a dripping bundle that had been pulled from the Serpentine in Hyde Park. It held a bride's silk dress, a pair of white satin shoes and a veil.
Inside the dress was a short note, calling the bride to come at once, signed with the letters F, H and M. Lestrade believed that they stood for Flora Millar, and he had already arrested her.

When Lestrade had gone, Holmes ordered a cold supper to be sent up and said that he expected some visitors. He told Watson that he had known the answer from the very beginning, and that the gown in the water proved nothing.

Soon Lord St Simon came back, and then the door opened and Hatty came in on the arm of a sunburned American. She told them that Frank Moulton had been her husband in the mining camp, and she had believed him dead for years.

Hatty said that she had never meant to hurt anyone, and that she had only wanted to run away with the man she loved. Lord St Simon bowed coldly and left the room in anger, and Holmes asked the lovers to stay and eat.
One snowy winter morning, a stout, well-dressed man rushed into Baker Street and dropped into a chair. He was Alexander Holder, a banker, and he looked like a man who had lost everything.

Holder explained that a client of the very highest rank had asked for a loan of fifty thousand pounds. As security, the client had left the Beryl Coronet, one of the most precious treasures in England.

Holder lived at Streatham with his son Arthur, his niece Mary and three servants. Arthur was a spoiled young man who gambled, and his friend Sir George Burnwell was charming, but Holder did not trust him.

That night, Holder lay awake, and at last he heard a sound that made him creep downstairs with a candle. In his room he found his son Arthur standing with the coronet in his hands, twisting it as if he meant to bend it.
Holder cried out that his son was a thief, and Arthur turned white and said that he could not explain. He would not tell where the three stones were, so Holder sent for the police.
Holmes agreed to look into the matter, and the two of them went by train to Streatham, with Watson at their side. On the way, the banker begged Holmes to find the stones and set his son free.

At the house, Holmes walked slowly round the garden and bent over the footprints in the snow. They told him that a man had waited at the gate, and that someone from the house had gone out to meet him.
Mary came into the hall, pale and tearful, and begged Holmes to save her cousin. She declared that Arthur was innocent, though she could not say how she knew it.

Dressed as a common loafer, Holmes spent the day in the lanes and the public houses, and nobody recognised him. He came back that evening, tired but content, with the three missing stones in his pocket.

Holmes explained that Mary had given the coronet to Burnwell, and that Arthur had followed them and fought to get it back. Arthur had said nothing to protect his cousin, and now Mary had run away with Burnwell.

Miss Violet Hunter was a young governess with a clear, determined face, and she had come to ask Holmes for advice. She had been offered a very good post, but she was afraid that it was too good to be true.

At an agency called Westaway's, she had met Mr Jephro Rucastle, a stout, jolly man with a heavy chin. He offered a hundred and twenty pounds a year to teach one small boy at his house near Winchester.

The catch was that Mr Rucastle wanted her to cut her long hair short and to wear a dress that he would choose. She would also have to sit wherever he asked, and she must follow every small order he gave.
Violet took the post, and she was met at the station and driven to Copper Beeches. That evening she cut her hair and put on an electric-blue dress that fitted her as if it had been made for her.
Mr Rucastle placed her in a chair beside the window, with her back to the road. Then he told such comic stories that she laughed until her sides were sore.
Mrs Rucastle was silent and sad, and her little son Edward was a spoiled boy who loved to hurt small animals. A huge dog called Carlo was kept hungry and was set loose in the grounds at night.
Violet hid a small mirror in her handkerchief and used it to look behind her. She saw a young man in the road gazing at the house, and Mr Rucastle seemed glad that her back was turned.
One day Violet searched her drawers, and she found a long coil of chestnut hair. It was exactly the colour and the length of the hair that she had cut off, and she could not understand it.
Part of the great house was unused, and Mr Rucastle forbade Violet to go there. One day she saw that Mr Toller was carrying food to a room in the empty wing, which he locked behind him.
One afternoon, Violet saw Mr Rucastle drive away, and she decided to look at the locked room. First, however, she sent a telegram to Holmes, because she knew that she might need help.
Holmes and Watson met Violet at the inn, and she told them all that she had seen. Holmes thought for a while, and then he said that she was being used to play the part of another young woman.
Mr Rucastle was away that night, and Toller had drunk himself into a deep sleep in the kitchen. Violet slipped the keys from his belt and led her two friends quietly toward the east wing.
They unlocked the oak door and found a bare room with a bed, a chair and a small table. A skylight stood open, and a ladder was set below it, so the prisoner had gone.

Just then the front door crashed open, and Mr Rucastle came storming along the passage with a lamp. He was purple with rage, and he shouted that they were thieves and that his daughter was his own affair.
Rucastle ran out and bellowed for Carlo to be let loose upon the intruders. But the great dog was starved and wild, and when it was loosed it flew at its own master's throat.
Toller woke up at the noise and ran in with a pistol. He fired, and the great dog dropped dead beside its master, who lay on the floor, badly torn.
When he was sober again, Toller told them the whole truth about the house. Alice, Rucastle's daughter, had been shut away because she would not sign away her money, and Toller had helped her escape.
The young man in the road was Mr Fowler, who had loved Alice for a long time. They were married by special licence at Southampton, and he soon took her to a new post in Mauritius.
As they rode home, Holmes looked out at the lovely fields and spoke in a quiet voice. He said that the lowest streets of London hid fewer sins than the lonely houses of the green countryside.
That night, Watson sat in the lamplight with his notes of the twelve adventures spread before him. In each of them, a clever man had shown that a little care could make a great mystery plain.

A moment later the lady herself ran out of the house and drove away after him in her carriage, and Holmes, who had no time to think, hailed a cab and followed them through the streets. Both carriages stopped before the Church of St Monica in the Edgware Road, and the lawyer and the lady hurried into the church. A quarrel broke out between some idle fellows outside the gate, and in the middle of it a man struck Holmes, who fell to the ground with red paint on his face. The lady ran out and ordered her servants to carry the kind old gentleman into her sitting room.

In an instant the room was full of choking smoke, and a number of people took up the cry in the street outside.
