At eight the next morning the King and the two friends drove to Briony Lodge, where an elderly woman met them at the door and said that her mistress had left that morning with her husband for the Continent. Holmes, startled at last, asked what had become of the lady, and he learned that she meant never to return to England. The King, who had already guessed that something was wrong, turned white and clutched at the door.

Holmes pushed past the maid, ran to the sitting room, tore back the sliding panel above the bell pull and plunged in his hand, and he drew out a photograph and a letter. The photograph was not of the King and Irene at all but of the lady herself, in evening dress and looking splendid. The letter, which was marked for Mr Sherlock Holmes to be left until called for, he tore open and read aloud to his two companions.

Irene's letter praised Holmes for acting so well that she had suspected nothing until the alarm of fire, but she had been warned against him long before, she added. As an actress, she wrote, she had often worn a man's clothes, and she had put them on, followed him to his door and wished Mr Sherlock Holmes good night. She and her husband, she explained, had thought flight the best answer to so formidable an enemy, and she assured the King that she loved a better man than he and would never use the photograph against him.

The King cried out with delight that Irene would have made a magnificent queen, and Holmes replied with dry politeness that she seemed to be on a very different level from His Majesty. When the grateful King offered him a ring in the shape of an emerald snake, the detective declined it and asked instead for the photograph of Irene Adler herself. Holmes had been beaten by a woman's wit, and ever afterwards he spoke of her under the honourable title of the woman.

One day in autumn Watson called at Baker Street and found Holmes deep in conversation with a stout, florid, elderly gentleman whose hair was of a brilliant, fiery red. Holmes, glancing at the visitor, remarked that apart from the plain facts that he had done manual labour, had been in China and had lately written a great deal, he could tell nothing more. The stranger, whose name was Mr Jabez Wilson, stared at him in open astonishment.

Holmes explained that the right hand of Mr Wilson was much larger than the left, which proved that he worked with it, and that the arc and compass on his pin showed him to be a Freemason. The shiny cuff and the smooth patch on his left elbow showed that he wrote a great deal, while a fish tattooed above his wrist and a Chinese coin on his watch chain told of a journey to China. Wilson laughed that at first he had thought it all clever, and then he saw how simple it was.

Wilson kept a small pawnbroker's business in Saxe-Coburg Square, near the City of London, and the shop did so little trade that he could hardly afford to keep an assistant. Two months earlier a man named Vincent Spaulding had applied for the post and had cheerfully agreed to work for half the usual wages, since he said he wished to learn the business. His one fault, said Wilson, was his love of photography, for he was always snapping with a camera and then diving down into the cellar like a rabbit into its hole.

One morning Spaulding handed his master the newspaper and wished aloud that he himself had red hair, for here was an advertisement of the Red-Headed League, which had a vacancy open to any man with red hair. The pay was four pounds a week for work so light that it hardly deserved the name, and the League, Wilson learned, had been founded by a dead American millionaire who loved red hair. Since he seldom went out, said Wilson, he was glad to hear any news of the world.

On the appointed morning Wilson shut up shop and went with Spaulding to Fleet Street, where the pavement was so crowded with red-haired men that he could scarcely believe his eyes. There were heads of straw, lemon, orange, brick and flame, and Spaulding, who had a gift for pushing, took him by the shoulders and drove him through the throng and up the steps of the office. It seemed to Wilson that all the red-headed men in London had gathered to claim a single post.

Inside the office Wilson found a little man whose hair was even redder than his own, who introduced himself as Duncan Ross, and who took hold of Wilson's hair and pulled it so hard that tears came to his eyes. He explained, apologising, that he had known cases of wigs and wax and dyes, and that the League had to guard against every kind of trick. Then, after a moment, he declared that nothing could be better and congratulated Wilson on being chosen from so many hundreds.

The duty, Ross explained, was simply to copy out the Encyclopaedia Britannica at a table in the office from ten until two every day, using pens and ink that Wilson must bring himself. He would forfeit the post for ever if he left the room even once during those hours, and neither illness nor business would be accepted as an excuse. Wilson, who found that Spaulding could easily mind the shop in the mornings, took the work and thanked his good fortune.

For eight weeks Wilson was faithful to his post, sitting at the bare table from ten until two, writing about Abbots and Archery and Armour and Architecture and Attica, and hoping that he might one day reach the letter B. Each Saturday Duncan Ross paid him four golden sovereigns, though he came less and less often to see how the work was going, and finally he stopped coming at all. It was a quiet, happy, well-paid life, and Wilson would not have changed it for any other.

One morning in the ninth week Wilson arrived to find the door locked and a small square of cardboard tacked upon it, which read that the Red-Headed League was dissolved and gave the date of the ninth of October. The landlord, an accountant on the ground floor, said that he had never heard of such a body, and that a solicitor named Morris had been the tenant and had moved away the previous day. At the new address, said Wilson bitterly, he had found only a manufactory of artificial knee-caps, where no one had heard of either Morris or Ross.

Holmes, who had listened with growing interest, asked Wilson to describe his assistant, and he learned that Vincent Spaulding was a small, quick, clean-shaven man, with a splash of acid upon his forehead and ears pierced for earrings. He sat upright with a start, and then, curling himself into his chair, he drew up his knees, put a pipe in his mouth and sank into a deep silence. Presently he rose and told Watson that this was a three-pipe problem, and that he must go to hear the violinist Sarasate at St James's Hall.

When the music was over, Holmes walked with Watson to Saxe-Coburg Square, a drab little place of faded shops and dirty railings, where he stood for a time in front of Wilson's pawnbroker's business. He struck the pavement several times with his stick, listening, and then he stepped up and knocked at the door. A bright, clean-shaven, clever-looking young man opened it and asked him to come in.

Holmes asked politely for the way to the Strand, and the young man named the turnings quickly and closed the door, which did not trouble Holmes in the least. He said that the fellow was the fourth smartest man in London, and that, for daring, he might even claim a place as the third. It was not the assistant's face that he had wanted to see, he told Watson, but the knees of his trousers.

By now Holmes was certain that the whole business of the League, and the copying of the Encyclopaedia, had been invented to get a dull pawnbroker out of his shop for several hours every day. While Wilson sat and wrote in Fleet Street, his assistant had been digging, night and day, in the cellar, and the tunnel was aimed at the vault of the neighbouring bank. The dissolving of the League meant that the work was done, and the criminals would soon be ready to strike.

Holmes had arranged for two helpers to meet them at Baker Street at ten, the first Peter Jones, a detective of Scotland Yard, and the second Mr Merryweather, a stern director of the City and Suburban Bank. The director, who grumbled that this was the first Saturday night in twenty-seven years that he had missed his game of cards, was never really sure that the matter was serious. Holmes assured him that the stake that night was larger than any rubber of whist, and the four drove off together through the dark streets.

Merryweather led the party through a passage and down a flight of stone steps into a huge cellar, whose floor was piled high with wooden cases. Inside them, he told Holmes, lay thirty thousand napoleons in French gold, which the bank had lately borrowed from the Bank of France, and the secret had apparently leaked out. Holmes asked for the lantern to be covered, and the four men crouched behind the crates to wait.

The darkness was so complete that Watson could hear each of his friends breathing, and the long hour of waiting seemed to him more like a week, with his limbs growing stiff and cold. At last a spark of light showed between two of the flagstones of the floor, and it widened into a yellow line. A white, almost womanly hand came groping up through the gap, and a head with a clean-shaven face rose into the lamplight.

The man pulled himself up and then reached back to help a second man out of the hole after him. Holmes sprang forward and seized the first by the collar, and when the man snatched out a pistol, his hunting crop came down upon the wrist, and the weapon clattered on the stones. The second man dived back into the tunnel and ran, and the cellar rang with shouts.

Jones laughed with delight, for he recognised the man as John Clay, a murderer, a thief and a forger, whose grandfather had been a royal duke and who had been educated at Eton and Oxford. The prisoner, quite unmoved, remarked that his friend had been caught at the other end, and begged that the police would kindly say sir and please when they addressed him. He bowed to them all, and with perfect composure he walked upstairs between two officers.

Over a quiet drink in Baker Street, Holmes explained that the advertisement had only one purpose, to get the pawnbroker out of his shop, and that the half wages and the cellar had shown him where to look. When the League was dissolved, he said, the work was finished, and it was likely to be used that very Saturday, since a Sunday gave the thieves a two days' start. The only question left was what they were digging for, and the neighbouring bank answered it.

Watson, filled with admiration, told his friend that the tale was a kind of triumph, and that he deserved the thanks of the bank and the police. Holmes replied lightly that his whole life was spent in one long effort to escape from the commonplaces of existence, and that such little problems were all the reward he wanted. The bank, he added, would pay his expenses, and for that he was grateful, but he could not eat admiration.

On a quiet evening Holmes stood at the window and told Watson that life is infinitely stranger than anything the mind of man could invent, and that the real world offers puzzles no author would dare to write. Below them a stout young woman in a large feathered hat swayed to and fro on the pavement, looking up at the windows. Holmes knew that signal at once, and he said that such uncertainty always means a matter of the heart.

The visitor introduced herself as Miss Mary Sutherland, and Holmes, after a swift glance, remarked that she must work at a typewriter, which had left its marks upon her sleeve. Her sight was weak, he added, since a pince-nez had left a dint on her nose. She confessed that both were true and, twisting her gloves in her lap, poured out the strange tale of the man who was to have married her.

Mary lived with her mother and her stepfather, Mr Windibank, a traveller in wines, who was barely five years older than she was and was often away in France on business. Her own father, a plumber, had died long ago, and a small yearly income left to her by an uncle in New Zealand was handed over to her family each month in return for her keep. She earned a little more by typing, and her stepfather did not like her to go out in the evening.

Against her stepfather's wishes, Mary went one night to the ball of the gasfitters, who had been friends of her father, and there she met a gentle, shy man named Hosmer Angel. He wore tinted glasses against the weakness of his eyes, spoke in a whisper because of an illness of his throat, and worked as a clerk in an office in Leadenhall Street. He called at her house the very next day, and from that visit a warm and serious friendship began.

Over the following weeks Hosmer walked with her in the evenings, but he avoided her stepfather, always calling while he was abroad, and he wrote her letters that were typed, even to the signature, and sent to a post office. He was a man of few words who disliked being seen, and he begged her to marry him at once and in quiet. He made her swear to be true to him, whatever might happen, even if something unforeseen separated them.

On the morning of the wedding Mary and her mother drove to St Saviour's in a hansom, while Hosmer followed alone in a four-wheeler, after he had begged her once more to be true. At the church the four-wheeler stood at the door, and the driver opened it, but the seat was empty, and Hosmer had gone as though the ground had swallowed him. He had been seen to get in, said the cabman, and no one ever found out where he had stepped out.

Holmes examined the letters with great care and noted that every one was typed, even the name at the bottom, which made them almost useless as proof of anything. He took down the address of Mr Windibank's firm, the importers of wine in Fenchurch Street, and told Mary to put the whole affair out of her mind. She replied firmly that she could never do that, because she had promised to be true, and she meant to keep her word.

When Mary had left, Holmes sat for a long time with his fingertips together and his eyes closed, and then he wrote a short, polite note to Mr Windibank at his office in Fenchurch Street. He asked him to call at Baker Street the next evening, and he told Watson that the matter was a simple one and that he already knew the end of it. The typewriter, he said, was almost as personal as handwriting, and every machine had small faults that a patient eye could learn to read.

Mr Windibank arrived punctually, smiling and a little too smooth, and Holmes laid his business letter beside the typed letters of Hosmer Angel and showed that the same worn letters appeared in each. He then locked the door and told the visitor calmly that he had invented a lover and played the part himself, in tinted glasses and whiskers, to keep his stepdaughter's money in the family. Windibank turned as white as paper, and for a long and dreadful moment he sat silent in his chair.

Windibank, still pale, said that he had broken no law and that Holmes had no proof that a court would accept, and he hurried to the door as soon as it was unlocked. Holmes took up his hunting crop in disgust, but the man was already running down the stairs and out into the street. He would not tell Mary the truth, he said, for she would never believe him, and he quoted an old Persian saying that there is danger in snatching away a delusion.

One morning a telegram came from Lestrade of Scotland Yard, asking Holmes to join him in the west of England on account of a tragedy in the Boscombe Valley, and promising that the air and the scenery were perfect. Holmes wished to take his friend, and Watson, who feared that he would only be in the way, was told by his wife to go. Within the hour the two had packed a bag and were driving across London to Paddington.

All the way from Paddington Holmes sat with his hat pulled down over his eyes and the newspapers piled up beside him, and he said hardly a word to Watson. At the little station of Ross, a neat, ferret-like man met them on the platform, and this was Lestrade, who had already engaged rooms for them at the Hereford Arms. He said that he knew Holmes would never be happy until he stood upon the very spot.

The dead man, Lestrade explained, was Charles McCarthy, who rented a farm at Boscombe Valley from a rich landlord named John Turner, and both of them had made their money in Australia. The two had come home to England at different times, and they were such old friends that McCarthy lived on Turner's land at a very small rent. McCarthy's only son, James, a lad of about eighteen, lived with him, and Turner's only child was a daughter named Alice.

On the afternoon of the third of June, Charles McCarthy walked down to Boscombe Pool, and a little later his son followed him carrying a gun. Patience Moran, a girl of fourteen who was picking flowers in the wood, saw them talking angrily, and James appeared to raise his hand as if to strike his father. She ran home in fright to tell her mother, and a few minutes later James rushed in, shouting for help.

James explained that he had been out shooting rabbits when he heard his father cry Cooee, the call that the two of them used, and that he had found him on the grass, badly hurt and barely able to speak. The dying man said something about a rat, he added, and when he looked up from his father's side, the grey cloak that he had noticed on the ground had disappeared. It was a poor story, said the police, from a boy who had been quarrelling with his father only minutes before.

That evening Miss Alice Turner called at the inn, pale but firm, and told Holmes that she had known James McCarthy since they were children and that he could never have done such a thing. Her father, she said, was ill and heartbroken by the news, and she was certain that the quarrel in the wood had been about something that nobody yet understood. Holmes listened to her carefully, and he promised to do all that he could.

By the lamp at the inn Holmes read through every paper that the police had collected, and he stopped over two small facts that nobody else had thought important. The first was that McCarthy had cried Cooee, which is a call used by the settlers of Australia, and the second was that his last words had not been a rat but the end of a name. Ballarat, he told Watson, was a town of Australia where both McCarthy and Turner had lived.

At the edge of Boscombe Pool, Holmes dropped to his knees with his magnifying glass and moved slowly over the grass, like a hound upon a scent, while Lestrade stood by and watched with a smile. He found the prints of the old man and of his son, and then those of a third person, which showed that a stranger had stood waiting beside a great grey stone. His face, which had been dull, shone with the keen look that Watson knew so well.

Beside the stone Holmes found the ash of an Indian cigar, a little mark on the stone itself, and a long stride of footprints in which the right foot made a shorter, lighter impression than the left. From the angle of the blow, he said, the man who struck it must have been left-handed, and from the stride he must be tall and lame in the right leg. He wore thick-soled boots, smoked cigars through a holder and carried a blunt pen-knife.

Holmes then described the murderer to Lestrade, a tall, limping, left-handed man in a grey cloak who smoked Indian cigars, and he advised the inspector to look for him in the neighbourhood of the pool. Lestrade laughed and said that he was a practical man, with no time for theories, and that the case against the young man was already complete. Holmes smiled quietly and said that each of them should follow his own method, and see which of them reached the truth first.

The next afternoon Holmes and Watson walked up to Hatherley Farm, the house of John Turner, and Holmes sent in a message that he must speak with the master. The old man received them in his study, a tall, white-haired figure with a stooping back, a deep limp and a grey cloak thrown over the back of his chair. Holmes looked at the cloak, and then at the man's left hand, and he said nothing for a moment.

Holmes said quietly that he had come to give the old man the chance to tell the truth himself, and that he would rather hear it from his own lips than be forced to guess at it. Turner stared at him for a long time, and then, with a groan, he covered his face with his hands and confessed that he had killed Charles McCarthy. He had not meant to hang an innocent boy, he cried, and he would speak if the lad could be saved.

In his youth in Australia, said Turner, he had been a leader of bushrangers known as Black Jack of Ballarat, and his gang had held up a convoy bringing gold from the mines. Among the drivers had been a young man named Charles McCarthy, who had been spared when the others were killed, and who had never forgotten what he saw. Turner had afterwards sailed home to England with his share of the gold and hoped that the past was buried.

Years later McCarthy had followed him to England, found him again and held his secret over his head like a sword, so that Turner had been forced to give him land at almost no rent and to bear his insolence. At last the bully had demanded that Alice should marry James, so that the McCarthys might inherit everything. Turner, who loved his daughter above all things, could not bear the thought, and he said that it drove him to the edge of madness.

On the third of June, said Turner, he had agreed to meet McCarthy at the pool, and McCarthy had called Cooee, as he used to in Australia, to tell him where he waited. They quarrelled again about Alice, and Turner, who had lost his reason, struck him down with a heavy blow. Then, hearing a step, he fled into the trees and left his grey cloak on the grass.

James, who had heard his father's last words and had seen the cloak, ran to the lodge for help, and in that short time Turner stole back, took his cloak and disappeared once more into the wood. That was why the police had found no cloak, said Holmes, and why the boy's story had sounded so strange. Turner agreed that it was the cause of all the trouble, and he wept for the harm that he had caused to an innocent man.

Holmes said that he was neither a judge nor a policeman, and that, if the boy went free, he would not use the confession against a man who had only a few months to live. Turner thanked him with tears in his eyes, and then, in a shaking hand, he signed a written account of the whole sad story. Holmes put the paper into his pocket and promised to keep it safe, and to use it only if the young man were condemned.

When the trial came before the court, the evidence against young James McCarthy was found to be thin, and the points that Holmes had put to the defence broke the case apart one by one. The jury found the prisoner not guilty, and the court was filled with the sound of joy as he walked out into the sunshine. Alice, who had waited outside, ran to him, and the two young people clung together.

Turner lived for about seven months after the trial and then died quietly in his bed, with the secret of his early life still known only to Holmes and Watson. James McCarthy and Alice Turner never learned of the dark cloud that hung over their fathers' past, and they were left to live in peace. Holmes, who had no need of thanks, kept the signed paper safe, and the case was added to his long book of memories.

On the train to London, Holmes sat silent for a long time, thinking of the old man who had been ruined by one wild moment and a lifetime of fear. Whenever he heard of such a case, he told Watson at last, he thought of the old saying, that there but for the grace of God goes Sherlock Holmes. Watson, who knew him well, said nothing, and the green fields of Herefordshire slipped away behind them in the evening light.

It was the end of September, and the gales had been blowing all day, so that the wind screamed in the chimneys and rain lashed the windows of Baker Street. Watson, whose wife was away with her mother, had come back for a few days to his old rooms, and he and Holmes sat reading by the fire. A ring at the bell was followed by the entrance of a tall, pale young man, dripping with rain, who said that his name was John Openshaw.

His uncle Elias, said Openshaw, had been a planter in Florida, had fought for the South in the American Civil War and had afterwards come to live in a lonely house near Horsham in Sussex. He was a hard, silent man who drank too much, seldom went out and kept an attic room locked, to which nobody was permitted to go. The young man had been allowed to live with him, and he had grown fond of the old fellow in spite of his temper.

One morning in March 1883 a letter with an Indian postmark reached his uncle, and when the old man broke the seal, five small dried orange pips rattled out upon his plate. On the inner flap were three letters, KKK, and the colonel, turning as white as death, cried out that his sins had at last overtaken him. He fled upstairs to his attic, and no entreaty from his nephew could persuade him to come down again.

The old colonel spent several days in a state of wild fear, burning the papers from a brass box that he kept in his attic, and then he made a will leaving his estate to Openshaw's father, Joseph. Seven weeks after the letter came, he was found lying face down in a small, green-scummed pool at the bottom of the garden, which was so shallow that no one thought he could have drowned by accident. The court called it suicide, though his neighbours knew that he had always dreaded death.

Joseph Openshaw took over the estate, and for nearly two years the family lived in peace, until a letter from Dundee brought five pips and an order to put the papers on the sundial. Within days Joseph was found dead at the foot of an old chalk pit, with injuries that seemed to come from a fall. The jury, who saw no sign of robbery or violence, called it an accident.

John inherited the estate, and for nearly three years he lived in peace, until, the day before, a third envelope arrived with five orange pips and the same message about the sundial. He had taken the letter to the police, who laughed at him and said that it was a practical joke, though he had read of the strange deaths of his father and his uncle. Now, he said, he was afraid for his own life, and he had come to Holmes.

Openshaw had brought a scrap of his uncle's diary that had escaped the fire, and it told of pips that had been sent to three men and of the quiet that followed their fates. Holmes told him gravely that the letters stood for the Ku Klux Klan, a secret society of the American South whose members had terrorised and murdered many people after the Civil War. The colonel, he concluded, had been one of them, had fled across the Atlantic with its records, and had been hunted ever since by those who wanted them back.

The three letters, said Holmes, had been posted in a port in India, in Dundee and in London, which suggested that the senders were travelling from port to port on a ship. He told Openshaw to go home at once, to put a note in the old brass box saying that his uncle's papers had been burned, and to leave the box upon the garden sundial as the letters had ordered. Openshaw thanked him, buttoned his coat and went out into the wind and the rain.

All night Holmes went through his index and the lists of shipping, comparing the dates of every vessel that had been in Pondicherry, Dundee and London, until at last his finger stopped on a name. It was the Lone Star, a ship from Savannah in Georgia, but in the morning the newspapers reported that Openshaw had been found drowned in the Thames at Waterloo Bridge. Holmes, who blamed himself bitterly, struck the table with his fist and swore that he would find the men who had done it.

Holmes learned that the Lone Star had left London on the morning after Openshaw's death, and he telegraphed to the police of Savannah in Georgia, describing the captain and the two mates who were wanted for the crime. In the end, the ship was lost in the great gales of the equinox, and nothing was found but a stern post marked with the letters L and S. That, Holmes told Watson, was one of the very few cases in which he had been fairly beaten.

Late one summer evening, when Watson was sitting by the fire with his wife, a ring at the bell announced Kate Whitney, an old friend, who burst into tears as soon as she was admitted. Her husband Isa, she explained, had been a slave to opium for years, and he had now been missing for two days in a den in the lowest part of the city. Watson, who was a doctor and had a kind heart, promised at once to go and fetch him.

The cab took Watson down to Upper Swandam Lane, a narrow and evil-smelling alley beside the river, and the driver set him down in front of a low door at the bottom of some worn steps. Inside, in a long room thick with brown smoke, he found the men lying in bunks like those of a ship's forecastle, some staring, some muttering and some quite still. The only light was the red glow of the pipes, and the whole place was the saddest sight in London.

Watson searched the room until he found Isa Whitney, who lay in one of the bunks, pale, haggard and shaking, with the empty look of a man who has given himself up to a drug. He took him by the arm, led him up into the cooler air of the street and put him in a cab that was waiting outside. It was not an easy task, but Whitney, weak and ashamed, did not resist.

As he turned to go, a low voice whispered in his ear, telling him to walk past it and then to look back, and a hand plucked at his sleeve. In the dim glow he saw that it belonged to an old man, bent and yellow, with a pipe hanging from his fingers, who seemed to be half asleep. Watson stepped past him, looked back, and then he almost cried out in amazement.

The old man was none other than Sherlock Holmes, who had made himself so pale and bent with the help of paint and padding that even his friend could not recognise him. He explained that he had been following the trail of a missing gentleman, and that he now needed Watson to come with him in his trap to the village of Lee, in Kent. Watson, delighted and astonished, watched the bent old man straighten his back, wink and become Sherlock Holmes again before his eyes.

Holmes drove out through the dark suburbs of the city until they reached The Cedars, a large villa standing in its own grounds in the village of Lee. Mrs Neville St Clair, whose husband had vanished, met them at the door in a light muslin dress with pink silk trimmings, and she was calm and collected. She asked eagerly whether they had any news, and she said that she could not bear to wait any longer.

Neville St Clair, his wife explained, was a respectable man in the prime of life, who had a good house, two young children, a fine income and not an enemy in the world. On Monday he had gone up to London by the train, saying that he had some business in the City and that he would buy a box of toy bricks for their little boy. She herself, as it happened, had business that afternoon in the city, where she had to collect a small parcel from the Aberdeen Shipping Company.

In the afternoon she had gone into the city to collect a parcel, and as she walked along Swandam Lane she heard a cry above her and saw her husband's face at a second-floor window. He seemed to be waving both his hands in great distress, and a moment later he was pulled back as if by some powerful grasp. She saw that he wore no hat and no collar, and she ran toward the door to find him.

She hurried into the building and up the stairs, but at the foot of them she was met by a sailor from India and a rough man who forced her back into the street. In the lane outside she met Inspector Bradstreet and some policemen on their rounds, and, with her help, they went up to the second floor. There they found no sign of St Clair, but only a strange and sinister beggar.

In the back room the police found Hugh Boone, a well-known beggar of Threadneedle Street, a repulsive man with a shock of red hair, a pale face and a scar that twisted his upper lip. He swore that he knew nothing of any St Clair and that he had been there all day. Yet the room held St Clair's clothes, and the child's present, a box of toy bricks, lay on the floor beside him.

The window of the room looked out over the river, and there were spots of blood upon the sill, and the tide, going out, had left St Clair's coat lying on the mud beneath. Its pockets were crammed with pennies and halfpennies, hundreds of them, and the weight had kept it from being swept away by the water. The beggar said that he had cut his finger, and the police believed that he had killed the missing man.

On the Tuesday morning, Mrs St Clair told Holmes, she had received a short letter that was certainly in her husband's handwriting. In it he told her not to be frightened, since all would come well, although there was a great mistake that might take time to put right. She begged Holmes to say that he was alive, and Holmes promised that he would think of nothing else that night.

Holmes gathered every pillow and cushion into a kind of Eastern nest and sat in it cross-legged, with an ounce of strong tobacco beside him, and he remained there silent and still until the dawn. Then, when the sun was just rising over the garden, he woke Watson, quite fresh and smiling, and cried that he had got to the bottom of it. Without another word he led the way down to the trap at the door.

The two friends drove through the quiet streets of the morning to the police station at Bow Street, where they found Inspector Bradstreet, a tall, stout, smartly dressed officer, who gave Holmes a warm greeting. Holmes explained that he wished to see the prisoner whom they had taken the day before, and the inspector, who knew his value, led them without delay down to the cells. The beggar lay in his cell in a deep sleep, with his face to the wall.

Hugh Boone lay sound asleep, as dirty and ugly as ever, with his shock of red hair and the deep scar that twisted his upper lip into a permanent sneer. Holmes remarked that he was a picture, and he asked politely for a basin of water, a sponge and a little help, and the amused inspector sent for them. Then, bending over the sleeper, he began to wash his face with the greatest care.

Holmes scrubbed and scrubbed, and then, with a single sweep of the sponge, the ugly scar came away with it, for it was only a strip of plaster, and the wig of red hair was lifted off. Underneath lay a pale, sad, refined face with black hair, and the man opened his eyes and sat up with a start. The detective, quite calm, said that this was Mr Neville St Clair of Lee, in the county of Kent.

The man covered his face with his hands, and then he admitted in a low voice that he was indeed Neville St Clair, and that he had never harmed a living creature. Bradstreet, who was struck dumb, said that the matter was a very serious one, since the man could be charged with a number of crimes. St Clair begged them, with tears in his eyes, to spare his wife and his children the shame of knowing that their father had been a beggar.

St Clair explained that he had been brought up at a good school and had worked as an actor, and then as a reporter for a London newspaper. His editor had once asked for articles on the beggars of the city, and he had made himself up with a wig, plaster and paint to find out how they lived. He had learned that a good beggar earned more in a day than he did in a week, and the money had been too tempting.

A debt that he could not pay had driven him back to the pavement, he said, and from then on he led a double life. Each morning he went to the City as a respectable gentleman, and each day he sat on a street corner in a ragged coat as Hugh Boone. He rented a room in Swandam Lane, above the opium den, where a kind sailor from India guarded his secret, and his wife believed that he held a good post in an office.

On that Monday afternoon, said St Clair, he had looked out of the window and seen his wife in the street below, and in his terror he had waved to her and then hidden. He had thrown the coat with its load of coins into the river and written the note in haste, sending it by his friend the sailor so that she should not be frightened. Bradstreet, who thought the man had learned his lesson, promised that the matter would be kept quiet if he gave up begging for ever.

On the second morning after Christmas Watson called at Baker Street to wish his friend the compliments of the season, and he found him lying on the sofa in his purple dressing gown. Within reach of his hand stood a wooden chair, and on it lay a very seedy and disreputable hard felt hat, cracked in several places. A magnifying glass lay beside it, which showed that Holmes had been studying it closely.

The hat, Holmes explained, had been brought to him by Peterson, a commissionaire who often did small errands for him, and it had a curious history. At about four o'clock on Christmas morning, Peterson had seen a tall man with a goose over his shoulder attacked by a gang of roughs in Tottenham Court Road, and the man had broken a shop window with his stick. Peterson had rushed to help, but the stranger, afraid of being taken for a criminal, had dropped his goose and his hat and fled.

A small card had been tied to the leg of the goose, bearing the words For Mrs Henry Baker, and the letters H and B were written in the lining of the hat. There were thousands of Bakers and hundreds of Henry Bakers in London, so that returning the property was no easy matter. Holmes had kept the hat, and he had sent the goose to Peterson's kitchen, since it would soon have spoiled.

Holmes held the hat to the window with his lens and told Watson that its owner was a man of high intelligence, since the hat was so large, and one who had been well off three years earlier. He had since fallen on evil days, said Holmes, and he had lost his foresight, and his wife, it seemed, no longer loved him, since the hat had not been brushed for weeks. He was also middle-aged, with grey hair that had been cut recently, and spots of tallow on the lining showed that he lit his house with candles and not with gas.

Holmes had hardly finished speaking when the door flew open and Peterson dashed into the room, with his face flushed and his eyes wild with astonishment. He held out one hand, and in the palm of it lay a small blue stone that blazed like an electric spark, which his wife had found in the crop of the goose. Holmes sat up on the sofa and whistled softly, for he knew at once what it was.

Holmes took the jewel between finger and thumb and held it up to the light, and he announced that it was the Blue Carbuncle, the most famous stone in London. It belonged to the Countess of Morcar, he said, and a reward of a thousand pounds had been offered by her for its return, which was not one twentieth part of its price. He added that the stone had a dark history of crime behind it, though it was only some twenty years old.

The newspaper told how the stone had been stolen from the Countess's room at the Hotel Cosmopolitan on the twenty-second of December, and how the jewel case had been found empty on her dressing table. A plumber named John Horner, who had been called to mend the grate, was arrested, and James Ryder, the head attendant of the hotel, had brought him to the room. Horner, who had been in trouble with the law before, declared that he was innocent, and he was waiting to be tried.

Holmes locked the jewel safely in his strong box, and he told Watson that the plumber might be innocent, for how could a man who had stolen the stone have put it in a goose in the street? Somebody had fed it to the bird, he thought, and the bird had somehow found its way to Henry Baker. To find the truth he must trace the goose, and for that he needed the man himself.

Holmes took a pen and wrote a short notice for the evening papers, asking Henry Baker to call at 221B Baker Street at half past six to claim a goose and a black felt hat. He sent Peterson to leave the notice at the offices of several newspapers, and then to buy a fresh goose to replace the one that had gone to his kitchen. It was a plain way of finding the owner, he said, and it would probably work.

At half past six Henry Baker arrived, a man with a large, intelligent head, round shoulders and a pointed beard of grizzled brown, and Holmes handed him the old hat with a bow. Holmes explained that the goose had been eaten, but offered him a fine plump one that lay on the sideboard, and Baker accepted it gladly. Over a glass he told them that the bird had come from the Alpha Inn, near the Museum, where the customers paid a few pence a week into a goose club and received a bird at Christmas.

As soon as Baker had left the room, Holmes said that the poor fellow plainly knew nothing about the stone, and that they must follow the goose while the trail was still warm. He put on his thick coat and wrapped a scarf about his throat, and the two men walked out into the cold, clear night. Their breath rose in white clouds, and the lamps of Holborn shone ahead of them.

At the Alpha Inn, a small corner pub near the Museum, Holmes ordered two glasses of beer and told the landlord that his geese were the finest he had ever eaten. The landlord, a pleased and cheerful man, said that he had bought them from a salesman called Breckinridge at Covent Garden market, and that they had been delicious. He did not seem to know, nor care, where the birds had been raised.

The great market of Covent Garden was nearly empty at that hour, and the porters were closing the shutters over the stalls, but at the end of a row Holmes found a light. There stood Breckinridge, a sharp-faced man with neat side whiskers, putting up the shutters of his stall, and he looked at the two strangers with open dislike. He said, with a scowl, that he was tired of being asked about his geese by every stranger in London.

Holmes, who knew how to deal with such a man, offered to bet a sovereign that the goose he had eaten was country bred, and Breckinridge snorted that the bird was nothing of the kind. He pulled out a greasy ledger to prove it, and Holmes read, under the name of Mrs Oakshott of 117 Brixton Road, a sale of twenty-four geese. Holmes paid the sovereign cheerfully, for he had learned exactly what he had come to find out.

As they were leaving, a small, thin, ferret-like man hurried up to the stall and asked in a whining voice about the geese that Breckinridge had bought from Mrs Oakshott. The dealer, who had been asked the same question a dozen times that evening, shouted that he had had enough of the whole business. Holmes followed the trembling stranger into the street, and after a hesitation the man gave his name as James Ryder and said that he wished to find a white goose with a barred tail.

In the cab neither man said a word, and at Baker Street Holmes sat the visitor by the fire, gave him a chair and a rug and told him that the goose had been in this very room. Then he drew the blue stone from his box, held it up to the light and said that the bird had laid an egg, and what an egg it was. Ryder's face went the colour of ashes, and he clutched the arms of the chair.

Holmes told the shaking man that he knew every link of the chain, from the first plan to the last. Catherine Cusack, the Countess's maid, had told Ryder that the plumber Horner was a man who had been in trouble, and the hotel attendant had seen his chance to put the blame on another. Ryder dropped on his knees and begged for mercy, crying that his mother would die of it, and swore with tears on his face that he had never done wrong before.

After the robbery, Ryder explained, he had hurried to his sister's house in Brixton Road, where she raised geese, and there he had picked out a fine bird with a barred tail and forced the stone down its throat. He had meant to carry it away at Christmas and then recover the jewel, but the goose had flapped back among the flock, and the one that he killed in his room had nothing inside it. By the time he hurried back to Brixton, his sister had already sent every goose to the market, and the stone was gone with them.

Holmes looked at the wretched creature, thought of the Christmas season and of the honest plumber in his cell, and then opened the door and bade him go at once. Ryder fled down the stairs and out into the street, and the sound of his feet rang along the pavement as he ran away from Baker Street. It was clear to Holmes that the man would never again dare to trouble the Countess or anyone else.

Holmes remarked to Watson with a smile that he was not employed by the police to supply their deficiencies, and that it was the season of forgiveness. A frightened man like Ryder would never steal again, he thought, and the plumber would be free as soon as the real story reached the court. He then asked Watson to ring the bell, since they could now begin another investigation in which also a bird would be the chief feature.

Early one morning in April, Holmes woke Watson and told him that a young lady had come to see them, in such a state of agitation that she could not wait until a decent hour. She sat by the fire in a thick veil, and she trembled so much that Holmes quietly told her to come close to the warmth. It was not the cold that made her shiver, she said, but terror, and she gave her name as Helen Stoner.

Helen lived at Stoke Moran, an old manor house on the western border of Surrey, with her stepfather, Dr Grimesby Roylott, who was the last survivor of one of the oldest Saxon families in England. The family had once been the richest in the land, but gambling and waste had ruined it, and only a few acres and the crumbling house remained. A single heir after another had lived in poverty, and Dr Roylott had gone abroad to study medicine.

In Calcutta the doctor had built up a large practice, but in a fit of rage he had beaten his native butler to death after a burglary, and he had narrowly escaped the gallows. He had spent a long time in prison and then returned to England, a morose and disappointed man. There he met and married the widow of a general, Helen's mother, who had two young twin daughters, Helen and Julia.

Eight years earlier their mother had been killed in a railway accident near Crewe, leaving her money to her husband for as long as the girls lived with him. Dr Roylott shut himself in the house, quarrelled with every neighbour and made friends only with the wandering gypsies, to whom he gave leave to camp on his land. He also kept a cheetah and a baboon, which roamed freely in the grounds and terrified the village.

Two years before, Helen continued, her sister Julia had become engaged to a major of the marines, and Roylott had given his consent, but two weeks before the wedding something dreadful happened. One night Julia came to her sister's bedroom at midnight and asked whether Helen had ever heard a low whistle in the dead hours of the night. Helen had not, and Julia went back to her room, though not before she had said that she could not sleep.

That night Helen heard a wild scream, and a clang as if a mass of metal had fallen, and then, running into the passage, she saw her sister stagger from her door with her face white with terror. Julia cried out that it was the band, the speckled band, and she pointed in the direction of the doctor's room, and then she fell, and in a few minutes she was dead. The doctors could find no cause for her death, though the room had been locked and bolted on the inside.

Helen was now engaged to be married herself, to a man named Armitage, and her stepfather had raised no objection. Two days earlier, however, workmen had begun to repair the wall of her room, and she had been forced to sleep in the very room in which her sister had died, and in the very bed. In the dead of the previous night she had heard, with a cold shock of terror, the soft whistle that had once been the herald of her sister's doom.

Holmes, who had been listening with his chin on his hands, asked her to show him her wrist, and he found upon it five little livid spots, the marks of four fingers and a thumb. Someone, he said, had treated her very cruelly, and she explained that her stepfather was a hard man who sometimes forgot his own strength. Holmes promised that he and Watson would come to Stoke Moran that same afternoon.

Soon after Helen had gone, the door of the room was flung open, and a huge man appeared, wearing a high hat and a long black coat, with a heavy hunting crop in his hand. His broad face, burned yellow by the Indian sun and covered with a thousand wrinkles, and his deep, bile-shot eyes gave him the look of a fierce old bird of prey. It was Dr Roylott, and he had followed his stepdaughter all the way to Baker Street.

The doctor shouted that Holmes was a meddler and a busybody, and that he was a dangerous man to fall foul of, and then, seizing the steel poker, he bent it into a curve with his huge brown hands. He flung it into the fireplace and strode out of the room, leaving the two friends alone. Holmes, laughing, said that he was not quite so bulky, but that his own grip was no weaker, and he straightened the poker with a single effort.

Holmes had first read the will of Helen's mother, and he saw that Roylott would lose most of his income if both girls married. At Stoke Moran, in the bedroom where Helen now slept, he found a bell rope that was not fixed to any bell, hanging beside a small ventilator that opened into the next room. The bed, too, had been fastened down to the floor, and it was in that very bed that Helen's sister had slept.

In the doctor's own room, Holmes looked carefully at the plain bed, the iron safe and the wooden chair that stood in front of the ventilator, and he picked up a saucer of milk from a shelf. There was also a dog whip with its lash tied into a small loop, and he said nothing as he turned it over in his hand. Watson saw by the glint in his eyes that he had begun to understand.

Holmes told Helen to complain of a headache that evening, to retire early and to place a lamp in the window of her old bedroom as a signal when her stepfather had gone to bed. He and Watson took a room at the Crown Inn, from which the house was in plain view, and they saw Roylott return, a huge, dark figure shouting at the boy who held the gate. Holmes told his friend that the hours before them were likely to be the most dangerous of their lives.

At eleven a single bright light shone from the window, and Holmes whispered that it was the signal, and the two friends crossed the lawn and climbed in at the window. Holmes laid his stick on the bed and Watson his pistol, and they sat in absolute darkness, listening to the chimes of the distant church clock. Holmes warned his friend to keep awake, for their lives might depend on it.

At about three in the morning a gleam of yellow light shone through the vent, and the smell of burning oil and hot metal drifted into the room. Presently there came a soft sound, like steam escaping from a kettle, and Holmes sprang from the bed, struck a match and lashed furiously at the bell rope with his cane. Watson heard a low, clear whistle, but in the glare of the match he could not make out at what his friend was striking.

A hideous cry rose in the house, a shriek of pain, fear and rage mingled together, and it was heard, they learned later, even in the village, where it woke the sleepers from their beds. Holmes and Watson stared at each other and then rushed into the passage and flung open the door of Dr Roylott's room. A dark lantern stood on the table, and in the beam of it the iron safe door was open.

Dr Roylott sat upright in his chair, wearing a long grey dressing gown and red slippers, with his chin raised and his eyes fixed in a dreadful stare at the ceiling. Around his brow was bound a peculiar yellow band with brownish speckles, which seemed to be tied tightly about his head. As they looked, the band moved, and Holmes whispered that it was the swamp adder, the deadliest snake in India.

Holmes quickly threw the noose of the whip round the reptile's neck, drew it from its horrid perch and carried it at arm's length across the room, and then he threw it into the iron safe and clanged the door. It was the creature that Roylott had trained, he said, and the doctor had died within seconds of the bite. Watson could not help thinking of the wretched man whose own plan had turned against him.

On the way home Holmes explained how the dummy bell rope, the ventilator, the bed fixed to the floor, the iron safe and the saucer of milk had led him to guess that a snake was used. Roylott had trained the creature to climb down the rope at the sound of a whistle and to return for milk, and the clang that Julia had heard was the safe shutting upon it. At first Holmes had thought of the gypsies' speckled handkerchiefs, but the dying girl's word band pointed to the snake.

Helen was taken to the care of an aunt near Harrow, and she put the terrors of Stoke Moran behind her. Holmes admitted that he was in a sense responsible for the doctor's death, but he did not think that it would weigh heavily upon his conscience. Violence, he told Watson, does recoil upon the violent, and the schemer falls into the pit that he has dug for another.

One summer morning, soon after seven, a railway guard whom Watson knew well brought a young man to his consulting room in Paddington, and the stranger sank into a chair, quite white, and fainted. When Watson unwrapped the handkerchief that was bound round his hand, he found that the thumb had been cut away, cleanly, at the base. The young man was Mr Victor Hatherley, a hydraulic engineer, and he had come up by the first train from the country.

When the wound was dressed and the patient had drunk a glass of brandy, he told his story from the beginning. He was a hydraulic engineer who had set up for himself in Victoria Street, and in two years he had had so few clients that he was close to ruin. Then one morning, just as he was thinking of closing the office, a thin, pale man with a hooked nose and a foreign accent arrived, giving his name as Colonel Lysander Stark.

The Colonel said that he wanted an opinion upon a machine that had developed a fault, and that he would pay fifty guineas for a single night's work, which was ten times the usual fee. There was only one condition, that Hatherley must tell no one where he was going, since the business was of a delicate kind, and he must take the last train to Eyford that night. Hatherley, who needed the money badly and had seen no such sum for months, could not possibly refuse so large an offer.

The train brought him at last to a tiny station, where there was one lamp, one porter and a black carriage that stood in the shadows, and there the Colonel was waiting. He hurried the engineer inside, and Hatherley noticed that the windows were of frosted glass, so that he could see nothing of the country through which they passed. The horses went at a great pace for what seemed an hour or more, and neither man spoke.

At last the carriage stopped before an old house with a dark porch, and a heavy door was opened at once by a stout little man in a coat. In the dim hall, a woman holding a lamp appeared, and she whispered to Hatherley in broken English that he must go away from that place before it was too late. The Colonel seized his arm and dragged him on down the passage, and the woman drew back into the shadows and was gone.

Stark took him into a small room in the middle of the house, where a huge iron press stood under a hanging lamp, and he explained that it was used to press fuller's earth into bricks for sale. It had lost power, he said, and a leak of water had been found in one of its cylinders. Hatherley, who was a clever and honest workman, set to work at once, and he soon found that a washer had worn out.

While he worked, Hatherley noticed a thin crust of shining metal on the floor of the press, and he understood at once that the machine was used for stamping not earth but metal. He guessed that the house belonged to a gang who made false coins, and he said so quietly to himself. At that moment the Colonel, who had been watching him keenly, saw the look of understanding on his face, and his own turned black with rage.

In an instant the Colonel had pushed the engineer into the chamber of the press and slammed the door behind him, and then Hatherley heard the heavy clank of the machinery starting. The great iron roof began to descend upon him, slowly, with a grinding sound, and there was no way out. He thought that it would be better to die at once than to be pressed into a flat shape by that engine.

When the roof was only a few feet from his face, the woman from the hall opened a hidden panel at the side of the chamber, and Hatherley, nearly dead with terror, threw himself through it. Behind him the roof crashed down upon the floor, and the whole machine shook. The woman, pale and shaking, pulled him by the sleeve and urged him toward the window of the passage.

Hatherley scrambled out of the window of the passage and was hanging from the sill by his hands when Colonel Stark rushed up with a heavy cleaver and struck at his fingers. The blow cut off his thumb at the root, and with a shout of pain he let go and fell into the garden. He knew nothing more after that, and he did not wake until the grey light of morning fell cold upon his face.

He awoke to a cold grey dawn and found himself lying in the dew at the foot of the garden hedge, with his wounded hand bleeding freely. He bound his handkerchief about the stump as tightly as he could, and the effort made the whole world swim before his eyes. The house behind him was perfectly silent, and he never knew whether the people in it believed him dead.

Somehow he got to his feet and stumbled through the garden gate into a narrow lane, where the first birds were singing in the hedges. With his bandaged hand held against his chest and the sky growing brighter above the trees, he followed the road toward the railway as fast as his weakness would allow. He had no thought but to put as many miles as possible between himself and that house.

At the little station of Eyford he was just in time for the first train of the day, and at Reading he changed for London. By the time he reached Paddington, he was so faint that a railway guard, seeing his white face and his stained handkerchief, led him to a doctor he knew. That was how he came to be sitting in Watson's consulting room, telling his story in the shaky voice of a man who had not slept.

Watson took the young man straight to Baker Street, where Holmes listened with his eyes half closed and his long fingers busy among the cuttings of a dozen newspapers. When the tale was done, he declared that it was the most remarkable story to have reached him in a month. Then he read out a notice that asked for news of a young engineer named Hayling, who had left his lodgings one night and had never been seen again.

He spread a railway map upon the table and made Hatherley tell once more how long the horses had run, how often the carriage had turned and what he had heard on the way. Holmes then said that a clever man would have wished to deceive his victim about the distance, and that a drive of an hour might have carried them no farther than a mile or two. If that were so, the house they sought could not be far from the little station itself.

Within a few hours the party was in a first-class carriage on its way to Berkshire, for Holmes had sent a note to Inspector Bradstreet of Scotland Yard, who joined them with a plain-clothes man. The map lay open across Holmes's knees, and he pointed out with a pencil the little station of Eyford. Hatherley sat opposite, pale and silent, with his bandaged hand held carefully against his coat.

As the train drew up at the platform, they saw over the roofs of the village a thick column of black smoke that rose slowly into the still air. A porter who was lounging by the gate told them, with the happy interest of a man who sees a spectacle, that a large house had caught fire an hour before. Hatherley caught Holmes by the arm, and his voice shook as he said that he knew the way.

It was an old, square house standing alone on a rise, and by the time the party reached the gate the flames had burst out through every window of the upper floor. A chain of villagers was passing buckets from a well, shouting to one another, though it was plain that nothing in the world could now save the building. Hatherley stood quite still among the crowd and said, in a low voice, that this was the very house in which the Colonel had shut him up with his machine.

The neighbours told Holmes that the fire had begun in a room in the middle of the house, where a lamp must have been overturned, and by evening nothing remained but a few black walls. In the soft earth of the garden, beside a hedge, Holmes found the prints of a large, heavy man and of a small woman, who had gone away together some hours earlier. Of the Colonel and his friends there was no other trace, and no one in the village knew anything about them.

In the train home, in the dusk, Hatherley sat rubbing his bandaged arm and said ruefully that he had lost his thumb, lost his fifty guineas and gained nothing whatever in return. Holmes threw back his head and laughed, and told him that he was richer than he supposed, for he had only to tell the tale at a dinner table to be welcomed in every house in London. Of the Colonel and his gang nothing more was ever learned, and the case joined the long list of Holmes's cases that were never wholly closed.

One wet afternoon in autumn, with the rain beating on the glass, Holmes sat by the window and read a letter that had come by the second post. It was written on thick paper and signed by Lord Robert St Simon, the second son of the Duke of Balmoral, who was to call at four o'clock upon a matter of the most delicate kind. A newspaper cutting told the rest, for it said that the lord had lately married Miss Hatty Doran, the only daughter of a rich American named Aloysius Doran.

Lord St Simon proved to be a tall, pale nobleman with a high nose, a stern mouth and the careful manner of a man who has always been obeyed. He told Holmes that the wedding had been a quiet one, with only a few friends, at St George's Church in Hanover Square, and that all had gone well until the very end. Then, he said, in a tone of complaint, the bride had behaved in a way that no lady of his own family would have thought of.

At the church the bride dropped her bouquet, and a gentleman who sat in the front pew picked it up and handed it back, and Lord St Simon thought that she looked pale. Afterwards, at her father's house in Lancaster Gate, a dancer named Flora Millar, who had once been a friend of the lord's, forced her way in and made such a scene that the servants threw her out. The bride was much upset by it, he said, and she asked leave to go to her room.

Soon after the breakfast began, the bride excused herself, went up to her room and came down again in a long coat and a plain bonnet. A maid saw her walk out of the front door and along the street, and it was said afterwards that she had been seen speaking with Flora Millar, though no one could be certain. By evening the guests had gone home, the wedding cake lay untouched, and the bride had not returned.

Holmes put question after question about the bride's past, and the lord answered each one with a growing air of offence. Hatty, it appeared, had spent her girlhood in the wild mining camps of the American West, where her father had made his fortune, and she was frank, high-spirited and impatient of rules. Lord St Simon seemed more wounded in his pride than in his heart, and when Holmes had done, he put on his hat and took his stiff leave.

Presently Inspector Lestrade came into the room with a dripping bundle in his arms, and he explained that it had been dragged out of the Serpentine in Hyde Park only that afternoon. It held a bride's dress of white silk, a pair of satin shoes, and a wreath and veil, all soaked through and dark with water. Lestrade was very pleased with himself, for he was sure that he had found the place where the lady had met her end.

Inside the dress was a short note which called the bride to come at once and which was signed with the letters F, H and M, and Lestrade was certain that they stood for Flora Millar. He explained that he had already arrested her, and that his theory was that she had lured the bride to the water and done her some dreadful harm. Holmes listened with a quiet smile, and then told him that he was looking for the lady in the wrong place.

Holmes went to the window, looked down into the wet street and wrote a short message that he refused to explain. He then ordered a cold supper to be sent up, and said that it would be required for a party of more than two, which puzzled Watson not a little. As for the gown in the Serpentine, he remarked, it proved only that a lady had taken off her wedding dress, and not that she had come to any harm.

A little before nine, Lord St Simon returned, stiff and cold, and a moment later the door opened and Hatty came in upon the arm of a sunburned American. She said, in a clear voice, that Frank Moulton had been her husband long ago in the mining camp, where he had been taken for dead after an attack by Apaches. For years she had mourned him, and she had married Lord St Simon believing herself free, until she saw Frank again, alive, in the church.

Hatty said that she had never meant to hurt anyone, and that she had slipped away with Frank because she did not know what else to do. Lord St Simon listened with a face of stone, declared that he had been very ill used, and left the room in cold anger. Holmes, who could not help feeling sorry for the lovers, asked them to stay and share the supper, and he told Watson afterwards that a cold dish is often the best way to soften a hard story.

One winter morning, while the snow lay thick in the street below, a heavy, well-dressed man came running along the pavement and burst into the room with wild eyes. He dropped into a chair, struck his head with his hands, and gasped out that he was Alexander Holder, a banker of Threadneedle Street. Holmes, who had seen many frightened men, said calmly that he must begin at the beginning and leave nothing out.

A client of the very highest rank, whose name Holder dared not speak, had come to the bank in need of fifty thousand pounds and had left as security the famous Beryl Coronet. It was a golden crown set with thirty-nine great beryls, and it was reckoned one of the most precious treasures in the whole country. The banker had been uneasy at keeping it in the bank's safe, and so he had decided to take it home to Streatham for the night.

At his house in Streatham, Holder lived quietly with his niece Mary, his son Arthur and three maids. Arthur had been spoiled since childhood, and he had run into debt at his clubs, and his friend Sir George Burnwell, a handsome, clever man of the world, was a guest whom Holder neither liked nor trusted. Mary, on the other hand, was gentle and sensible, and she had always kept the household cheerful.

Holder, who slept badly, was lying awake in the night when he heard a faint sound that seemed to come from his dressing room, and he crept down the stairs with a candle in his hand. There he found his son Arthur, in his shirt and trousers, standing beside the open bureau and holding the coronet, which he seemed to be twisting with all his strength. A corner of the crown had been broken off, and three of its beryls were gone.

Holder cried out that his son had robbed and disgraced him, and Arthur, standing with the broken crown in his hands, turned very white and said that he could say nothing at all. He would give no account of the missing stones, whatever his father pleaded, and when the police arrived at last, he allowed himself to be led away without a word. Holder, half mad with misery, said that he cared nothing for the fifty thousand pounds and that he cared only for the truth.

Holmes asked a few short questions about the household and then agreed to take the case, and a little later the three men were in a train bound for Streatham. The banker spoke all the way, pleading that his son must be set free, for he could not bear to think of Arthur in a cell. Holmes listened, and said only that the facts seemed to point in one direction and the heart of the banker in another.

Before he entered the house, Holmes walked slowly round it with his eyes on the ground, studying the snow like a hound on a trail. The ground had been trodden by many feet, but he soon sorted out one man who had waited long at the gate, and another person who had come out of the side door to meet him. He said that one thing was already clear, that the coronet had not been stolen by a stranger who broke in.

Mary Holder came into the hall, pale and tearful, and she begged Holmes with clasped hands to set her cousin free. She declared, with a certainty that seemed strange in so gentle a girl, that Arthur was innocent, though she could give no reason for it. Holmes listened politely, asked a few quiet questions about the servants and the side door, and then said that he wished to see the rooms upstairs.

Dressed in a shabby coat and with a battered hat pulled low, Holmes spent a whole day in the lanes and the taverns, talking with idlers and listening to gossip, and not one of them guessed who he was. He returned late in the evening, muddy and tired but very satisfied, and he laid on the table the three missing beryls, which he had bought back at a heavy price. Holder gave a cry of joy, and a moment later he wrote out a cheque to cover the cost.

Holmes explained that Mary, who had fallen under the spell of Sir George Burnwell, had taken the coronet at night and handed it to him. Arthur, who had seen it all, had run out after the thief and wrestled with him in the snow, and in the struggle the crown had been bent and the three stones lost. Holder, weeping, learned that Mary had left a letter and gone off with Burnwell, and he begged his son's pardon for ever doubting him.

Violet Hunter was a young governess with a quick eye and a firm chin, and she had come to Baker Street in some distress of mind. She had been out of work for some weeks, and now an offer had arrived that was so generous that it frightened her more than it pleased her. She wished to know, before she answered it, whether Holmes thought she could safely accept.

At the agency she had met a Mr Jephro Rucastle, a large, jovial man with a great deal of chin and a smile that seemed fixed upon his face. He offered her a hundred and twenty pounds a year to teach one small child at his house, Copper Beeches, a few miles from Winchester, which was more than twice what she had ever been paid. It was the sort of offer, she said, that makes a careful person look for the catch.

The conditions were so strange that she had at first refused, for he wished her to wear any dress he gave her, to sit in any chair he chose, and to crop her hair very short. When he saw that she meant to go away, he raised the salary, and at last he promised that nothing he asked would be unreasonable. Holmes said that he would not have a sister of his own go to such a house, but that she must send a telegram at any hour if she needed him.

In spite of Holmes's doubts she accepted the post, and a fortnight later she was met by Mr Rucastle's trap and driven to Copper Beeches, a great house that stood among a ring of copper-coloured trees. That evening, with a heavy heart, she let Mrs Rucastle cut off her long chestnut hair, and then she put on the dress of electric blue that lay ready on her bed. It fitted her so perfectly that she could only suppose it had been made for someone of exactly her size.

Mr Rucastle led her to a chair set near the window, so that her back was turned toward the road, and he began to walk up and down before her, telling the most ridiculous stories she had ever heard. She laughed until her sides ached, but Mrs Rucastle, who sat by without a smile, never so much as looked up from her work. After an hour of this, he told her that her duties for the day were done, and that she had done them well.

Mrs Rucastle was a thin, silent woman who seemed afraid of her own husband, and her little boy Edward was a spoiled child who delighted in hurting small creatures. The only servants besides the cook were Mr Toller, a coarse man who smelled of drink, and his wife, who was as silent as her mistress. A great mastiff called Carlo was kept half starved and let loose in the grounds after dark, and Violet was warned, with perfect seriousness, that she must never go out at night.

One morning Violet, who had begun to feel that her back was being used for some purpose, took a small mirror from her handkerchief and held it up as though she were wiping her eye. In the glass she saw a man in a grey suit standing in the road and looking toward the window, and he seemed to be in a state of great distress. Mr Rucastle at once told her to move the chair and to sit facing him, so that the stranger should not see more than the back of her head.

Soon afterward, while she was looking through a locked drawer of her chest, she found at the bottom of it a long coil of chestnut hair tied with a ribbon. She laid her own cut tresses beside it and found that they were exactly the same in colour and thickness, which was so strange that she could scarcely believe it. She put the lock back with great care and said nothing of it to anyone in the house.

The east wing of Copper Beeches, she was told, was not in use, though one of its doors, of heavy oak, showed signs of being often opened and closed. One day she saw Mr Toller carry a tray along the passage and unlock this door, and then she heard from within the sound of someone moving. When she asked about it, Rucastle's face darkened, and he told her that it was a lumber room.

When a letter came from Mr Rucastle's friend, which called him to town for some days, Violet decided that this was her moment to learn the truth. Before she made the attempt, she walked to the village and sent Holmes a telegram, for she felt more strongly every hour that she was in the middle of something wrong. The answer came at once, and it told her to do nothing rash and to wait for him at the inn.

Holmes and Watson reached the village inn that same evening, and Violet told them everything, from the blue dress to the coil of hair and the tray that was carried to the east wing. Holmes listened without a word, his eyes shut and the tips of his fingers pressed together, and at the end he said that he believed he understood the whole of it. Someone was being kept in that locked room, he declared, and Violet had been brought to Copper Beeches to play that person's part before the eyes of the man in the road.

Mr Rucastle was away in town that evening, as Violet had hoped, and Toller, who drank every night as soon as his work was done, lay snoring beside an empty bottle at the kitchen table. Violet drew the heavy keys quietly from his belt, and then she led Holmes and Watson, who had come in at the back, along the dark passage toward the east wing. The great house was as still as a church, and far away across the lawn they could hear the restless pacing of the mastiff.

Holmes opened the oak door, and in the light of his lantern they saw a bare room with a bed, a chair and a table, and a skylight standing wide open overhead. A ladder had been set under it, and a thick rope of knotted sheets still hung over the sill. The bird, Holmes said quietly, had flown, and someone had come to help her.

At that moment they heard the front door slam, and Mr Rucastle, who had returned early from town, came storming along the passage with a lamp in his hand and his round face purple with rage. He shouted that they were thieves, that they had no business in his house and that his daughter was his own concern. Holmes answered him in a cold, steady voice that his daughter was nowhere in the house, and that he had better think of the law before he spoke of thieves.

In his fury, Rucastle ran out to the back of the house and bellowed for the dog to be let loose upon the intruders. The great mastiff, which had been kept half starved for months to make it savage, came bounding across the passage, and it went straight at the man who had shouted. Rucastle fell back with a dreadful cry, and the dog's great jaws closed upon his throat.

The noise had roused Toller from his stupor, and he ran in with a pistol in his hand, sobered by the sight before him. He fired twice at the mastiff, and the animal rolled over with a groan, while Rucastle lay on the floor torn and bleeding, with the lamp smashed beside him. They carried him to a bed and sent for the doctor, and Watson did what he could until help arrived.

Toller, who was now perfectly sober and looked ashamed of his past, told Holmes the whole story in a low voice. Alice, who was Rucastle's daughter by his first wife, had been shut up in the east wing for months, because she would not sign a paper that would have given her father control of her fortune. Toller had always pitied her, and that night, with his wife's help, he had put the ladder to the skylight and let her out to her friend.

The man in the grey suit was Mr Fowler, to whom Alice had been engaged, and he had refused to believe that she had forgotten him, even when he saw a laughing girl at the window. With Toller's help he had carried her away that very night, and within a few days they were married by special licence in Southampton. Soon afterwards, he took his wife to a new post in Mauritius, where she could live free of her father.

As the train carried them back toward London, Holmes looked out at the pleasant farms and the little villages with their smoking chimneys, and for a time he said nothing at all. At last he remarked that the lowest alleys of the city do not hold a more dreadful record of wickedness than the smiling and beautiful countryside, where a crime may go unseen for years behind a hedge. As for Violet Hunter, he added, she was soon to be the head of a private school at Walsall, and she deserved every success.

That night, in the quiet of the study, Watson sat in the lamplight with his notes on the twelve adventures spread out before him, from the masked King of Bohemia to the blue dress at Copper Beeches. He thought of the red-haired man, the vanished bridegroom, the five orange seeds, the beggar with the twisted lip, the goose and its jewel, the speckled band, the missing thumb, the lost bride, the broken crown and the starving dog. Across the room, Holmes sat in his chair with his violin on his knee and the pipe at his side, and Watson knew that he would not have changed any of it.
